speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. It arises out of a statement which the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) reportedly made outside the House last evening. During a special debate yesterday, the minister had an opportunity to make an announcement on what he would do regarding beef prices in this country. However, no announcement of new policy was made by the minister in the House last evening.
Earlier in the week the minister promised that such an announcement would be made sometime this week. Last evening I drew this to his attention, as did other members, but we received no response. The minister then went outside this House and reportedly made to the press a specific commitment on two aspects of the motion before the House. I believe it is an infringement upon the rights and privileges of all members of this House for any minister of the Crown to refuse to announce a new policy in the House and then speak to the press outside, while the debate is in progress, and announce two new aspects of a policy which he should have announced in the House.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON LEGISLATION CONCERNING $500 GRANT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a statement concerning forthcoming legislation. I should like to confirm the government's intention to introduce in the House very soon legislation which would authorize, for a one-year period, the payment of a $500 grant to people buying a new home for the first time, provided the home is moderately priced. For this purpose a home may be defined as a principal residence of permanent type which conforms to local standards or by-laws.
This measure was a commitment made by the government during the election campaign in order to make it easier for families to purchase their first home. Rather than wait until legislation can pass through the House, I wish to make this benefit available to families immediately and to remove any uncertainty on the part of the home buyer or the housing industry.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to advise the House and the people of Canada that when this legislation is presented to hon. members for their approval, it will stipulate that the grants will be payable to people who fulfil the required conditions and who purchase and occupy their new homes on or after this day, November 1, 1974, until November 1,
1975.	In other words, the legislation, if approved, would be retroactive and would benefit people who bought and occupied their new house now, without waiting any longer.
The conditions under which the grants may be paid will be spelled out in the legislation but I would like today to review our intention in general terms.
The homeowner grant would be payable to people who are buying a new home for the first time, within price limits which vary by market area. They will be those used by CMHC in setting the upper limit of loans it will insure under the National Housing Act. In Regina, for instance, the grant would be payable to someone buying a house costing $31,580. In Toronto, where costs are substantially higher, the maximum price eligible for a grant would be $44,915.
The legislation will provide that the housing must be new, not previously occupied and must be the owner's principal residence. At such time as the legislation may be approved, the owner who has bought and occupied his new home may apply to the local Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation office which would process his application and, if it is acceptable, send him a cheque.
This grant will be a selective measure, Mr. Speaker, directed to those who need help. As the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) pointed out in announcing the government's intention:
It will go directly to the home buyer-to the consumer. It will not be available to housing speculators or to the wealthy purchasing expen-
November 1, 1974

sive homes. It will be -available to first time buyers of moderately priced homes.
I hope, Mr. Speaker, that this legislation will find favour among hon. members when it is presented as a timely help for a very large number of Canadian families. It is an important initiative in the broad range of federal housing measures and one of a number of proposals which I shall be presenting to the House during this session of parliament.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON LEGISLATION CONCERNING $500 GRANT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should first of all like to thank the minister for sending me a copy of his statement. I received it about a quarter to eleven and I would have been concerned if there had been very much in it, particularly with a housing crisis of the proportion that we have today.
At the outset I might say that I am very happy to get some confirmation at least on this matter, because when the House first convened for this parliament I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) about this promise and he sort of threw up his hands and gave one of those evasive answers to the effect that within the next four or five years some legislation would be introduced.
I think we must take a look at this program. First of all it provides $500 to anyone who purchases a new home at a moderate price. Those are important words when you analyse the degree of inflation in this country and in the United States today. As one of my friends pointed out a few minutes ago, the present rate of inflation is about 10 per cent so that the price of a house in the category set out in the second paragraph of the statement would increase from between about $4,000 to $5,000. Keeping that in mind, this is really not going to do very much to assist these people.
I should like to ask the minister one question through you, Mr. Speaker, about this most unusual procedure. If this government is as honest, as credible and has the degree of integrity it attempts to hold out why did the minister not present a bill today for first reading? In this way we would not only know that the $500 is to be provided for by legislation, but we would then have the opportunity to see the law and the regulations regarding the manner in which this money would be paid.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON LEGISLATION CONCERNING $500 GRANT
speechtext: He is not ready.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON LEGISLATION CONCERNING $500 GRANT
speechtext:
Of course, the reason we have received a statement rather than a bill is that we have flushed this government out. During the election campaign it made about $2.5 billion worth of promises across this nation. I suggest the only person who really has not had a heart attack over this is probably the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner), who is too busy trying to wiggle out of these promises.
Why was a bill not presented in order that we might know the terms and conditions of this proposal? I suggest today we have a very serious housing crisis. This matter is so important that I should like to spend a few minutes on it. It is interesting to note that on October 2, I posed a question concerning the drop in housing starts of 24.3 per cent over last year. In fact, housing starts for September
Housing
were down 35 per cent. When I brought these figures to the attention of the new minister he said, as reported in Hansard for that date at page 28:
-I suggest there is not a housing crisis in this country.
When the minister held a press conference, and I draw this to his attention, he said, and I quote from the Vancouver Province of October 21:
Danson says he's "about to present new ideas to cabinet" to help solve the housing mess.
That statement was made about the time he was denying in the House that there was any mess or crisis. I do not know whether anyone can take him seriously when, at one time he holds a press conference at which he states there is no mess, while at another time he admits in the House that there is. Perhaps the minister has gone to his colleague the Minister of Finance with his cap in his hand. In any event, he is always talking about AHOP under which $467 million has been spent. I understand there is about $47 million to $50 million left under that program, so it is about to die when there is an actual housing crisis in this country.
Unless this government comes to grips with ever increasing inflation, high interest rates and the fact that the average man, even with both he and his wife working, cannot afford the down payment on a new house, this program which is really a government subsidy program, will go bad. If it merely provides the $500 to the developer or the builder and not to the purchaser, and I am concerned about that, it might be known as the "rotten egg" housing program. I suggest it will be about as effective if the grant goes to the developer or the builder and not the purchaser, and that is our fear.
It would have been far more effective had this government repealed the 11 per cent sales tax on building material, and that would be far more realistic.

We found out by examining the estimates that nothing was really being done about land banking in this country. No money has been spent on the new demonstration program, and I suggest if there had been this would not have built even one new house. In any event, if the money is being spent that program is costing the country $55,000 a day without one new house for anyone and without any real effect in curbing the housing crisis. My final word on this matter is that the minister should go back to his colleagues for some concrete policy that will curb inflation, and in that way he will be doing something about the housing crisis in this nation which he denies exists.

What we need to solve the problem is action to increase the supply of houses, action with regard to decreasing the interest rate and action with regard to the diffusion of moneys to increase the land banking and the servicing of lots across the country.
With regard to increasing the supply of houses we have had an announcement that there will be a 25 per cent drop in respect of housing starts this year. With regard to interest rates no action whatsoever has been taken to decrease the interest rates. May I remind you, Mr. Speaker, that if a person were to buy a home with a $35,000 mortgage at 11 per cent it would take him 25 years to pay if off at a rate of $350 a month. After 25 years, he would have paid $100,000. This action does nothing to help the serious housing crisis across the country. We need action. Members of the New Democratic Party have mentioned that there should be a revolving fund with regard to land banking, and there should be a massive infusion of money for the servicing of land across the country so that more housing may be available.
This is a miserable offer to solve the housing crisis across the country. When one looks at the restrictions related to the $500 grant, one finds that it must be a new house and that the person involved must be a first-time purchaser. Then, there are the limits with regard to price. The limit the minister mentioned in respect of Regina would be $31,580 and the limit in respect of Toronto would be $44,915. The average price of a house in Toronto is $55,000. I would invite the minister to take me to any place in Toronto and show me a new house that could be purchased for a price of $44,000 or less.
This is legislation by announcement. If the minister wanted to bring forward this meagre measure, why could he not have translated it into legislation immediately and have it passed. He does not want to do it. He wants to spin it out and be a part of this slow progress for which the Liberal government is so well noted. As I said, this minister is not a minister of housing but of hoaxing. This is a cruel hoax on the purchasers of homes in Canada. I would remind the minister that the philosophy announced by his predecessor is that every Canadian is entitled to a home at a reasonable cost. This minister is not implementing that philosophy. It is about time he stopped this hoax and took the initiative with regard to this serious problem.

Mr. Speaker, I have heard and read the statement made by the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Danson) in which he says that only first-time buyers of new moderately priced homes can benefit from the $500 grant for a moderately priced home of $31,850 or a $44,915 home in Toronto.
Mr. Speaker, I sincerely believe that this statement and the legislation which we eventually will have before us is a sheer mockery at the population. Indeed, of the ordinary workers who constitute the very broad majority of our population and who earn $8,000, $9,000 or $10,000 a year, who are those who can afford a $44,000 or a $31,000 house? It is true that it is somewhat impossible to buy anything cheaper these days, but that does not mean that it is a moderate price; it is rather a prohibitive one. That is the

problem. And we will not assist home ownership with a legislation providing for a $500 grant for people buying a new home, when the sales tax on building materials stays at 11 per cent. That means about $3,000 on any house within the categories mentioned by the government.
There is another point. When a Canadian citizen buys a home and seeks financing with banks or Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to whom he has to pay a 12, 13 or 15 per cent interest rate, instead of the 7 or 8 per cent interest rate of yesteryear, Mr. Speaker, what is the $500 good for? There will not be, I believe, 2,000 people across Canada who will avail themselves of this legislation. That means that the government is still laughing at the worker, at the Canadian population. And if they were logical in their dealings with people, they would first suppress the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials and bring down the interest rates to 5 per cent, instead of demanding 15 or 18 per cent as the case is presently.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING THE ADMINISTRATION OF INTERPROVINCIAL. EXPORT AND IMPORT TRADE IN PETROLEUM AND PETROLEUM PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I moved the adjournment of the debate yesterday I had outlined five proposals which might become part of a national oil policy for Canada. I want now to add a sixth proposal. I believe the government should not tie up scarce capital and materials on oil and gas pipelines mainly designed to move United States oil and gas to the United States, which will have little value for Canada. The first of these proposals, and I know it is now being resurrected, is for the construction of an oil pipeline from the Mackenzie Valley to the United States. It should be pointed out that we do not, so far, have any proven reserves of oil in commercial quantities in the Mackenzie Valley. The main purpose of such a pipeline would be to transmit oil from Prudhoe Bay to the United States. It is true that if we discovered some oil we could put it into that pipeline, but the quantity of Canadian oil would be negligible and would not warrant the $6 billion to $10 billion capital investment that would be required.
The same thing is true with reference to a gas pipeline from the Mackenzie Valley to the United States. In this instance we do have commercial quantities of gas in that area, but we have a 25-year supply of gas in the southern part of Canada and we need not look at this area for at least ten years. Those who are proposing the building of a gas pipeline from the Mackenzie Valley are not thinking in terms of Canada's need. The situation is that the gas in the Prudhoe Bay area can only be taken out as the oil
Oil and Petroleum
resources are exploited; therefore, they want a pipeline with Canada involved so that for the first four or five years some 70 per cent or more of the gas going through the pipeline will be Canadian gas. The result will be that by the time we need the Arctic gas most of it will have been sold, through the Mackenzie Valley pipeline, to the United States. There will come a time when we will need that pipeline, but that is some years away. When we build such a pipeline, it should be a pipeline to sell Canadian gas in Canada, and not to export it out of the country.
My third point has to do with offshore oil reserves. So far we have not, unfortunately, found quantities sufficiently large to warrant development. We cannot count on this source to solve our problems in the next decade. It is to be hoped that oil will be found off the Atlantic coast, but we should reconcile ourselves to the fact that in this respect a lead time of five to ten years will be required. Therefore, Canada's best bet is to develop the Athabasca oil sands and the heavy oil deposits in Saskatchewan. The estimate is that the Athabasca oil sands have an oil capacity of some 300 billion barrels, of which about 50 billion barrels can be recovered by strip mining. The National Energy Board report of 1972 suggested that we could produce 1,200,000 barrels a day by 1985. It is my opinion that this figure is too optimistic as it would mean building eight plants between 1977 and 1985 and moving about two million tons of loose quartz sand every day. I do not think that is possible. We must step up the programs we have now.
What concerns me is that the government seems to be lackadaisical about the one sure source of oil to meet the critical situation which will confront us between 1979 and 1980. We already have the Great Canadian Oil Sands company, which is producing some 53,000 barrels a day and which will probably go up to a peak of 65,000 barrels a day. We have the Syncrude plant which is now under construction and is hoped to be completed by January, 1978, with a capacity of 125,000 barrels per day. Also, the Shell Oil plant, if it proceeds as it should, will be started in 1976 and completed in 1981, also with a capacity of
125,000	barrels per day.
If we assume an exportation and importation balance, I think it is safe to say we will have to find a supply from other sources. The only other sources which come to my mind are the Athabasca oil sands and the heavy oil deposits in Saskatchewan. We will have to find, from those sources, between 300,000 and 400,000 barrels a day by 1980, and something over 900,000 barrels a day by 1985. That is the reason I urge that we do everything possible to step up the program in respect of the oil sands and the heavy oil deposits.
First, I think our course of action must be by way of conservation in order that the existing, conventional oil supplies will last as long as possible. Second, we must step up, encourage and intensify the development of oil from the oil sands. Third, the government should be spending very large sums of money now in scientific research related to alternative sources of energy, because we must not forget that even the great oil deposits of the Middle East have a life index of only 35 years. The whole question of solar energy, geothermal energy and nuclear power must

November 1, 1974
Oil and Petroleum
be examined, and the research must be carried on much more rapidly than has been the case.
I am concerned about the provisions in this bill for paying compensation to the oil companies and for paying higher prices to the gas companies. Canada is paying tremendous sums of money to the oil companies for imported oil. We agree that it is necessary to maintain a single price across the country, plus transportation and handling charges. But we paid out, under Governor General's warrants, between June and October $470 million in compensation to the oil companies. Under this bill, for the first quarter of 1974 the government is authorized to pay out another $430 million. This will represent an amount of $900 million in a period of less than a year.
I have a very strong feeling that the public funds of Canada are being ripped off by the oil companies. It is very significant that, in this oil crisis, everybody makes some sacrifice except the oil companies. The consumers have accepted an increase of $2.50 a barrel. The provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan are giving up in the order of $1,300 million a year. But the oil companies have never had it so good. The profits of Imperial Oil increased 45 per cent last year over 1972, after payment of taxes. The profits of Gulf Oil, after taxes, increased last year by 58 per cent over 1972. I do not have their figures for 1974, but I do have them for Shell. In the first nine months of this year the Shell Oil company had profits of $119.5 million, compared to $60 million for the first nine months of last year. This represents an increase of almost 100 per cent. It is positively obscene, at a time when we face a national and an international crisis, that the multinational oil companies have been able to rip off the public and the public treasury to the extent that they have.
This legislation allows the government to fix the price of gas. I do not object to that, because this party is in favour of selective price controls. This is one field in which price controls are appropriate. We want to know, however, the price level that the minister has in mind. In statements which have appeared in the press from time to time the minister has suggested that the price probably ought to rise from, say, 60 cents per thousand cubic feet to $1.20 per thousand cubic feet, by stages-on the principle, I suppose, that it does not hurt a dog if you cut off his tail an inch at a time. Why does the price have to virtually double over a period of time? Have the costs of production gone up? No one will quarrel with an increase in price if the costs of production have risen, but they certainly have not risen to the extent the minister seems to envisage.
I do not buy the argument that it is necessary for these companies to have larger and larger profits because they will use those profits to explore for more gas. If the government wants them to use the money for the exploration of gas, let the provinces and the federal government collect the money and then rebate it to them for the exploration they carry out or, better still, have the exploration carried out under federal and provincial auspices. I think the public will accept higher prices for gas if production costs warrant it, or if they can be sure the money will be used to find further supplies. But the public will not stand for an increase in the price of gas if it is merely to swell the already high projects of the gas companies and of TransCanada Pipe Lines in respect of the

transportation and sale of resources which belong to the people of Canada.
I wish to make an appeal to members of this House, particularly the younger members, many of whom will be here long after I have left. I ask that, no matter what their party is, they apply themselves conscientiously to finding a solution to the energy crisis which faces Canada and the world. This is the most serious problem facing our generation. I suggest that the policies we adopt and the actions we take in the next few years will determine our life style, our future and our survival.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING THE ADMINISTRATION OF INTERPROVINCIAL. EXPORT AND IMPORT TRADE IN PETROLEUM AND PETROLEUM PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I always appreciate the opportunity to take part in a debate on energy, which is so important to the economy of my province which produces about 86 per cent of the crude petroleum not only for domestic needs but for export to meet the needs of the world. I also like to follow the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas). Even though we may disagree on our stand in respect of a program, he always provides food for thought and has vision. I was pleased to hear him speak out as he did today, particularly in his concluding remarks, about this being one of the most serious problems facing Canada and the world in the next few years.
I am told by representatives of the industry in Calgary that they now find, since the election-probably because the pressure is off-that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) has relaxed a good deal, is much more affable and easier to deal with. I hope that situation continues for the next four years. I should like to break my speech into four parts. I wish to deal with the history of this bill, some of the constitutional questions involved, and particularly part III of the bill. I also wish to say a few words in respect of incentives for exploration and development, which is one of the most important aspects of this subject, in order to ensure an adequate supply.
The bill, in part, flows from the historic meetings of first ministers. That was a point made by my friend, the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton). We all remember the second last meeting of first ministers, held at the residence of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in the latter part of March, 1974. We need not wait for history to put that occasion into proper perspective, as the agreement they reached will stand as a triumph of statesmanship, good sense and co-operation in the delicate field of federal-provincial relations. I heard the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain say that.
I would emphasize another point which was made by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain; that is, that when the meeting took place and there was agreement, it was for a period of 15 months. That is why we have grave reservations, with which I will deal later, in reference to part III of the bill, whereby the federal government can bring about price-setting, control of supply and other measures without consulting the provinces and securing their agreement. Of course, if you carried the practice to its logical conclusion, it would destroy the economy and the jurisdiction the provinces have under the constitution. The essence of the agreement was that for a period of 15
November 1, 1974

months, which would expire on July 1, 1975, the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan undertook to sell one of their principal, non-renewable resources at an average price-as the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands said-of $6.50 per barrel at the well head. There would be a set price across the land, except for such factors as transportation and handling. The federal government, for its part, agreed to adjust the distribution to ensure that crude oil would become available at the same basic price across the country.
Part III of this bill was not one of the terms of the government reached by the ministers but was, rather, a mechanism whereby the federal government, by agreement in cabinet, could impose its will unilaterally upon the producing provinces in respect of the price at which they would sell one of their depleting natural resources. To that concept, strong exception has been taken by myself, by the attorney general of Alberta and by members of the standing committee when Mr. Leitch appeared before them as a witness, both on the ground of principle and of constitutional validity.
Part III, to which our most fundamental objections are directed, far from embodying a term of first ministers' agreement, stands as a direct negation of the principles upon which that agreement was based. It permits the executive council to terminate an existing agreement between a producer province and the federal government, or to decline to negotiate a renewable agreement and to impose, by unilateral action, maximum prices on a natural resource owned by the province.
The inequities in part III are both plain and subtle. I ask the minister-even though his party now has a working majority in the House and in the committee, so that when I said what I did about the industry, it was not puffery; it was fact-in view of the new atmosphere in which the minister is operating, is he giving serious consideration to making changes to part III? If he is, this bill could be expedited, not only on second reading but in the committee. If one of the negotiating parties reserves unto itself the right to cancel the bargain, or the right not to bargain at all, then the consultative or negotiating process becomes meaningless: the concept, the grand scheme, the sensible formula for resolving federal-provincial differences loses its very foundation. For example, if one of the negotiating parties, by legislation, purports to reserve unto itself powers of the most dubious constitutional validity, it invites the other party to embark upon a course of judicial confrontation.
There was a position taken early in the negotiations and the minister knows that even the proposition to implement the surtax may be questionable constitutionally. The producing provinces-I do not know whether it was Mr. Blakeney of Saskatchewan or Mr. Lougheed of Alberta- did not want to come to the federal government at a time when there appeared to be problems and a constitutional confrontation before the Supreme Court of Canada; therefore they arrived at the agreement which I have already discussed.
In the last analysis, when viewed in practical terms, part III amounts to an assertion by the federal government of the right to regulate the price, the flow, the production and the sale of a provincial natural resource. I
Oil and Petroleum
say that is unconstitutional. It embodies a concept which I am sure no provincial government, after measuring the consequences of its extension to other natural resources this is the point the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain was making-such as lumber and hydro power, would accept. I do not believe for one moment that a powerful province in central Canada which has more political muscle than others because of the number of its members, the province of Quebec, would want to see a federal tax put on hydro, which they export, particularly in view of the great development at James Bay. I think somebody said last night that what is sauce for the goose is sauce for the gander. If we do not have equality for all provinces, small and large-those with small representation and those with large representation-on matters of this nature, then confederation will erode.
We deal with potash, iron ore, asbestos, nickel, copper and coal without acknowledging that in today's economic circumstances the federal government has taken complete charge of the provinces' capacity to determine their future economic development. I am sure that was never intended in the terms and conditions of confederation, even in the spirit of confederation, and it is certainly not in the spirit of the law as it has been interpreted. There is no need for the legislation contained in part III which provides for the substitution of the federal will for the negotiated agreement referred to in part II. They can negotiate, they can make agreements for the good of the nation even when they represent the special interests of their province, which every provincial premier must do.
The first ministers' conference demonstrated the presence, strength and vitality of the national concept in a way which is perhaps unparalleled in our history. I hope that concept will not be impaired by the enactment of legislation which is unnecessary and susceptible to constitutional challenge because, as I have said, the very spirit of confederation would be eroded. I do not think now is the time, when we are dealing with matters of energy, to have a constitutional confrontation.
I might say that in the area of constitutional law-and the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands, who was the premier of Saskatchewan for many years, will agree with me-when you are interpreting the constitution before a judicial tribunal, everything depends on the personalities there. I do not want to pass any judgment that would reflect upon a judge, but I say that the personality of a man appointed to that position, and his philosophy when he is interpreting the constitution and therefore taking into account the social, economic and political implications, is reflected in the decision. That is why, whether it is in the Supreme Court of Canada or the supreme court of the United States, you find that the courts legislate in the field of constitutional law.
I do not know who mentioned this, but it has been said that it seemed to be constitutionally unsound for the provinces to tax little, but constitutionally sound for the provinces to tax much. Surely that is not the formula on which we should base federal-provincial relations when dealing with taxation, particularly when dealing with property, civil rights and resources owned by the provinces.

November 1, 1974
Oil and Petroleum
I should like to turn for a few moments to a matter that has political implications. In May, 1974, gasoline prices increased. The higher gasoline prices, following the controlled lifting of the price freeze by the federal government, reflected the increased cost of doing business but mainly the higher cost of the raw material, namely, crude oil. Very little of the price increase went to the petroleum industry; most of it ended up in the government treasury. I make one suggestion, if we want to put safeguards on this: if you leave it to the corporations, human nature being what it is they can use the money for exploration in Canada, all things being equal in international competition. I agree with the suggestion of the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands that if oil companies are to be encouraged to explore and develop petroleum resources, the government should in some way hand back to them part of the money which has been paid in tax, as compensation for exploration expenses. Only in this way will we encourage exploration and development of petroleum and natural gas.
State-owned corporations are not as efficient as private corporations. True, some corporations have made agreements with communist countries, but they remain privately owned. I do not think a state-owned company can be as efficient as a privately owned company which is answerable to its shareholders. That is where I part company with the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands. I accept his first idea, that of giving a rebate to companies for exploration expenses, but I reject his second idea. We differ in philosophy in that regard.
What is the future of the Canadian oil situation? Canada will be threatened with the loss of self-sufficiency in crude oil production toward the end of this decade unless action is taken now to increase investment in new oil resources. The word which keeps cropping up as I listen to members of this government and of provincial governments is "supply." That word is very important in any consideration of the price of crude petroleum. Adequate supply will only come about through adequate exploration and development.
Many geologists in my constituency believe that there is much oil still to be found in Saskatchewan and Alberta. People speak as if no more oil is to be found there. They are not right. In addition, we have the tar sands and we have the Arctic development, about which I shall speak later. What is most serious is that drilling rigs are moving out of this country because greater incentives for exploration are provided elsewhere. These rigs always go where the action is, where the dollars are. Let us be practical. I have yet to meet a man or a woman who can tell me that human nature is different as between Socialists, Conservatives and Liberals. We are all pretty much the same.
What is our Canadian oil potential? There is much guessing, but it is estimated that our potential reserves total over 300 billion barrels, enough to meet Canada's needs far into the future. We can only develop this potential if we encourage exploration. This we can do only if we change some of our ideas with regard to taxation. This, too, I shall speak about later. What happens when there is a cutback in oil production, or in exploration and development? The adverse effects are felt not only in Calgary,

which city people have already left, but in the rest of Canada in the secondary and tertiary industries which operate in areas like the golden horseshoe and other industrial areas. For example, the oil industry buys from Ontario manufacturers piping and valves worth between $500 million and $600 million. So when you rock the boat it is like disturbing the balance of nature. The ripples spread out and are felt in every corner of the land.
What can one say about oil industry profits? Some say that these profits are excessive, relevant to investment in the oil industry. Others who have examined the facts say that returns are not very great. I will deal with this topic later. The $6.50 per barrel price of crude oil provides only 77 cents per barrel investment for oil companies with regard to search and development. In other words, out of the gross price of $6.50, the companies have available 77 cents to invest in exploration and development in Canada, unless cash flows in from outside. Many of us think that some degree of Canadian investment is preferable to foreign investment. Well, you cannot cut the profit levels of oil companies to nothing and expect them to carry out exploration and development. So I suggest that there is a need for foreign capital and we must develop a sensible formula in this regard.
Provincial and federal governments, through the medium of the export tax, take about 90 per cent of the value of exported oil. As we heard yesterday, the federal government had received by June 1974, $900 million in oil funds, and by the end of this year it will receive $1.5 billion. Most of our oil comes from Alberta. Saskatchewan exports to the United States most of its 14 per cent share of production. From its 86 per cent share of production, Alberta supplies all areas of Canada west of the Ottawa Valley. We are providing oil to the rest of Canada at $6.50 per barrel when the world price is better than $10 per barrel. As the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain said, what Alberta is doing shows that the province is not selfish. It is subsidizing eastern and central Canada to the tune of $1.5 billion. Altogether, in one year the 1.5 million people of Alberta will subsidize the rest of the people of this country to the tune of $3 billion.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, we have a little quality here today, if not quantity. Before lunch I was dealing with the fact that with the surtax alone that is collected on Alberta resources, $1.5 billion is paid to subsidize and compensate for the cost of oil imports, mainly from the Middle East and Venezuela. In addition, $1.5 billion is paid
November 1, 1974

to Ontario indirectly by reason of the fact we are selling crude petroleum to them at $6.50 a barrel: it is the difference between $6.50 and the world price. The surtax has been as high as $5.20. Our profits are compensating the nation in respect of crude petroleum in the amount of $3 billion annually. That is the amount collected this year. I know the minister agrees with that figure.
I wish to turn for a few moments to the consumer problem. It is at the gasoline pump that the public meets the petroleum industry most frequently, not in the executive offices. It is, therefore, only natural that public reaction to petroleum industry activities begins at this point. Yet the gasoline pump is many steps removed from the raw material source, the oil well, and it is even more remote from the planning and legislative process that controls the search for and development of the raw material. Therefore, there sometimes is not very much liaison between the consumer who fills his car with gasoline, and the people involved in the exploration and development stage. When I talk about that stage, I need only remind the House that this week a tragic accident occurred. Thirty-two people from PanArctic, with know-how and skills, geologists and others, lost their lives in the Arctic this week through exploration and development for our nation.
Any burden on the raw material, be it in the form of royalties for the provinces, royalties for the federal government, surcharges, mineral tax or corporate tax, must eventually be borne by the consumer. He is the only real taxpayer. I emphasize that: royalties, surcharges, mineral taxes and other taxes must eventually be borne by the consumer. Taxes are just as much a cost of doing business as are wages, salaries and raw material. If taxes on the raw material increase, the cost of the raw material will in turn rise and the consumer will pay higher prices at the gasoline pump. I want to emphasize that we cream so much off the resource industry that we do not leave enough money in Canada for exploration and development. Our explorers and developers are engaged in international competition. Corporations which are owned by Canadians, the drilling companies, will leave Canada.
When Canadians began paying more for gasoline following the controlled lifting of the price freeze on petroleum by the federal government on May 15, 1974, the higher prices reflected the increased cost of doing business, but mainly the higher cost of the raw materials. Very little of the price increase went to the petroleum industry; most of it ended up in government treasuries. As I have said, Mr. Speaker, there was an increase of $2.50, from $4.00 to $6.50. Of that $2.50, the oil companies received about 77 cents; the rest went into government treasuries to be used for various programs, federal and provincial.
The proposals in the budget of May, 1974, would, if implemented, accentuate this situation. The point I am trying to drive home once again is this: if the May budget had been approved, or if the same terms and conditions are included in the next budget, the federal government would be taxing not only the profits of the companies but the royalties paid by them, royalties which constitute a provincial tax. In other words, these royalties are included in the amount upon which tax is claimed by the federal
Oil and Petroleum
government. I say that this is unconstitutional, that it is unfair and that it is certainly not good for confederation.
Inherent in such a process is the prospect of an energy shortage in the near future. Consumer dollars siphoned off by governments into the social sector are not available to the industry for reinvestment in finding, developing and producing new supplies of oil. What will happen? In the end, Canadians will be the losers. There are people in this House who seem to enjoy the prospect of a shortage of crude petroleum. They talk about an energy crisis. Mr. Speaker, there never was a real energy crisis in Canada. What we saw, resulted from the inability of governments to plan transportation and pipelines to move petroleum and natural gas to all parts of the country at a cost which the people and the industrial empire of Canada could afford. There certainly was not a shortage of supply. If there is a shortage, how is it we are exporting a million barrels of crude petroleum to the United States every day? As things are, the consumer faces the prospect of paying increasingly high prices while at the same time Canadian supplies dwindle and Canadian self-sufficiency is impaired.
When you tax an industry to death, the consequences are obvious-exploration slows down and the cost of gasoline at the pump goes up. Canadian crude oil production from the so-called established areas will soon peak and then begin to decline if there is no further exploration and development, especially of the tar sands. We shall become increasingly dependent upon foreign supplies. Canadians are not used to such a disturbing outlook. Under the stimulation of a national oil policy backed by appropriate tax and royalty policies, Canada tripled its oil production from 625,000 barrels a day in 1961 to two million barrels in 1973. This was the program devised and implemented by the government headed by my right hon. friend from Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker).
Members on the treasury benches opposite have often spoken in glowing terms about the national oil policy implemented by the party to which I belong, a policy which, as I say, enabled us to triple our oil production. If we could do that in a ten-year period in the past, we can do so again. The fear that we shall run short of supplies is not great. The fear of Canadians who understand this question is that pea-brained policy makers will fail to provide an incentive for the development, the supply will fall off and the cost of energy to the consumer will go up.
I want to deal, now, with the world situation as it fits into the picture, with special reference to OPEC and how it works. OPEC is not a government, but a world power which is presently giving the western world the jitters. And it shows no sign of breaking up. The welfare of most of the world's non-communist countries depends more and more on decisions made by a dozen oil producing countries acting through a cartel, plus Venezuela and Ecuador. Who are the members and leaders of this suddenly powerful group? How are they able to make the oil consuming world pay ransom? OPEC's full name is the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries. The source of their power is oil, billions of barrels of it, and the billions in dollars and other currencies which have come from its sale. It is the source of their power and their common bond.

November 1, 1974
Oil and Petroleum
Incidentally, Mr. Speaker, they never put their own money into the development of these resources. It is foreign capital which developed these wells in the Arab countries as well as in South America. Be this as it may, OPEC is rapidly becoming one of the most powerful cartels the world has ever known, controlling the price and supply of oil which is the lifeblood of industrialized societies. In the last 12 months some members of the cartel, acting individually, have restricted the output of crude. All its members, working together, have been able to impose an increase of 400 per cent in the price of crude oil as a result of the stranglehold they have exercised over this vital resource. Indeed-and I speak after giving this matter a great deal of study and attention-this stranglehold exercised over a large part of the world's energy resources has raised fears of a global depression resulting from the growing burden of oil costs. Such a depression is well within the realm of possibility in the next few years.
It is obvious to anyone who comprehends international trade in crude oil petroleum that the wealth of the industrial western nations is fast flowing to the Arabs. The seriousness of the situation is starting to sink into the consciousness of all western nations, including Canada. Unless we can create a climate and atmosphere for continued exploration and development, a deep global depression is in the making, caused in large measure by the astronomical increase in price of crude petroleum in the last 12 months, an increase from $2 a barrel to $10 a barrel. At one point the price was $11 a barrel.
The blackmail and economic pressures caused by the OPEC countries cover the Mesopotamian area, plus South America. Let us consider some of the high costs that have resulted. In 1973 the United States imported the same amount of oil as in 1974; the cost in 1973 amounted to $7.5 billion, whereas the cost in 1974 is estimated to be $25 billion. Japan paid $6.7 billion in 1973, and $21 billion in 1974. West Germany jumped from $5.1 billion to $11 billion, France from $3.4 billion to $9 billion, Britain from $3.3 billion to $9 billion, and Italy from $2.1 billion to $7 billion. Canada imported proportionately less, but nevertheless it cost us an extra $1.5 billion. This sum was paid, not by the treasury but from revenue derived from the resources that flow from the province of Alberta. Only 16 per cent of our oil emanates from Saskatchewan, and this is used for their own consumption.
The finance ministers of the western world, including the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner), gathered in Washington in early October for a meeting of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank. All western countries were worried that they would not be able to pay their inflationary oil bills or would not be able to borrow enough to pay those bills, and they asked the producing nations, particularly OPEC, to lend money to the World Bank from the surplus of moneys they had earned from oil sales. The serious question is, will they do this? If they will, then will they continue to do it?
Canada has been in a very fortunate position, however, and will continue to enjoy that position provided the federal government does not overkill exploration and development. I emphasize the word "overkill" in terms of taxation, which stymies exploration and development.

Every day we use from our own crude reserves one million barrels, and we export about the same amount to the United States. In other words, we import one million barrels and export one million barrels. So our imports and exports of crude petroleum are equal. Therefore, Madam Speaker, in reality we are self- sufficient in oil and would face no problem if this government and the provincial governments would make certain that transportation facilities will carry these reserves to all parts of Canada. The propaganda that Canada had an oil crisis, as I have said, was manufactured by the government to cover up for its ineptitude, procrastination and vacillation.
Those who oppose foreign capital coming into the resource industry are the first to cry blue ruin when there is a shortage. You cannot develop this type of industry without large pools of capital. Everyone seems frightened to say this, but I am not: if it had not been for United States capital and know-how at the beginning, in 1947, Alberta would not be in a position today to supply 86 per cent of domestic Canadian crude petroleum needs and, in addition, export one million barrels a day. We must always remember-I say this without criticism-that the money to develop these fields of oil did not come from St. James Street in Montreal any more than it came from Bay Street in Toronto. The money came from a foreign source to begin with. We were as poor as any other non-producing province until Leduc No. 1 was drilled in 1947. The development took place ten years after a world depression, at a time when Alberta could not meet even the interest of its bonds.
In other words, all the finance ministers were told that the western world must come to grips with this problem or we would definitely be in a serious recession or depression. It is regrettable that a country which continues to build reserves by developing the tar sands and encouraging continued exploration within provincial borders and the Arctic is following a policy of overkill in development. The OPEC price will only be reduced when countries like the United States, as the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowi-chan-The Islands said today, find alternatives to crude petroleum and, indeed, natural gas.
This does not mean that a worldwide economic slump is unavoidable. But it does mean that there is no single, simple solution, and from what I have read, and according to what independent financial experts in the world say, the answer for Canada lies in exploration and development in Canada. If we had ample supply at a time of shortage, then for the first time we would be able to outcompete our competitors. This means a great deal, particularly to the province of Ontario which is the industrial centre of Canada and which has transformed us from an agrarian nation to an industrial one.
All the beautiful arguments about the constitution may contain many high-sounding phrases, but I have found that in the field of constitutional law, constitutional tribunals legislate by interpreting words to fit the social, economic and political conditions of the time. Therefore, precedents and constitutional law are of somewhat limited value.
I should just like to refer briefly to two other matters. Some 39 rigs and 250 crewmen left Canada this year in response to the great demand in the United States and the
November 1, 1974

Middle East. One has only to read what Mr. Thomas Kennedy wrote in the Globe and Mail to learn how many drilling rigs are leaving Canada because of the overkill to which I have referred. They are going to the United States, Alaska, the North Sea and elsewhere. Our enemies-I mean our political enemies-will in the future be able to rise in this House and say that we are now in short supply because of the short-sighted policies of the government. Preliminary statistics as at the end of September indicate that 2,967 exploratory and development wells were completed in western Canada, including the Arctic, for a decrease of 245 from the first three-quarters of 1973, and there was a decrease in footage to 10.6 million feet. Those figures speak for themselves.

First of all, we must make certain that our corporations are good citizens. On the other hand, we should stop flogging business for emotional vote-getting. One thing of which I am confident is that corporations are here to stay. Farm-out agreements with corporations in communist countries are common.
