To digress, I must say he is a better golfer than I am. Canada cannot, and will not, destroy these corporations. Our rules should be set up and shaped in such a way as to make certain they offer these corporations incentives in a competitive world to continue their development and exploration operations. The federal attempt to tax every barrel of crude petroleum, taking into consideration royalties in the calculation, means tax upon tax, and this must be abandoned. Section 36 of the act must be modified so that the federal government does not have the power to control supply, price-setting, and so on, without consultation with and agreement of the provinces. In addition, I think a North American conference should be called in order to have either formal or informal discussion of the best ways to develop and explore our resources and, indeed, find alternative crude petroleum on the North American continent. We must remember we are in competition with the European Common Market and the Asian bloc.
Lastly, the subsidy paid to the provinces which are importing crude petroleum should, in my opinion, come from the taxpayers' federal treasury, instead of the government continuing to gouge revenue out of one or two
Oil and Petroleum
provinces. I end on the words I used in starting. I thought the greatest statesmanship was shown when the provincial premiers came together with the Prime Minister and his ministers to work out a deal to sell oil at $4 a barrel less than the price of the same oil in the world market. I could not help thinking of the bigotry of some people when I read the following in a leading newspaper recently:
If Alberta can exploit the accident of geological history that left much of Canada's oil and gas within the boundaries of the province, then surely it cannot complain when central Canada exploits the accident of Canadian history that gave it sufficient political power to dominate federal politics and determine that national policies shall favour the east.
That is real bigotry, because we reached a compromise with the rest of Canada to make sure that this nation would get its energy at a proper and equitable price. I have enough faith in this country and in the provinces of Quebec and Ontario to say that they have not, to my mind, ever deliberately used the power that has been given them to break up and destroy confederation. The answer today may lie in energy to help this great nation build together for the future. I thank hon. members for giving me extra time and I say it has been a pleasure to talk to hon. members this afternoon.

speakeroldname: Mr. Maurice Foster (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING THE ADMINISTRATION OF INTERPROVINCIAL. EXPORT AND IMPORT TRADE IN PETROLEUM AND PETROLEUM PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am very happy to have the opportunity to speak to Bill C-32, the Petroleum Administration Act. I was very interested in the comments of the hon. member for Qu'Ap-pelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) and the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas). I think the wind-up statement by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands, when he spoke about the energy issue as perhaps being the most important to be decided in this session of parliament, was very true. The energy policies we adopt in the next few months or the next year or so will have a very important effect on our life style, the growth of this country, our attitude toward growth and our ability to compete in the world marketplace. I was pleased to note, as well, that the hon. member agreed with most parts of this bill. Most of the remainder of his speech seemed to me to deal with other matters which are important, but outside the scope of the bill before us this afternoon.
I listened with great interest to the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain, for two reasons. I lived for a few years in his constituency, and know what a fine constituency it is and the importance of that part of Canada. I listened, also, because that hon. member has a reputation in this House of being a man with ideas and I wanted to see what new ideas he would bring before us. It seems to me that a couple of his ideas were not altogether accurate in respect of this bill. He suggested that the former bill which this one replaces, Bill C-18, was a much more temporary measure that would be phased out automatically. As I read it, that is just not the fact. There was no time limit or specific time when Bill C-18 would pass out of existence.
The hon. member also suggested that Bill C-32, the one before us, was a whole new ball game and a completely different bill. I submit that nearly all its features, includ-

November 1, 1974
Oil and Petroleum
ing the export charge, the oil pricing system, the system of restraint on oil prices, the compensation program and the administration of the act are basically the same as those in Bill C-18, with only the addition of gas pricing and the procedure of compensation features of this bill being new. Even here, the principle of restraint in gas pricing and the prescribing of a gas price is the same as that outlined in Bill C-18 in respect of oil.
It seems to me that the hon. member was agreeing with the idea of cushioning the transition to higher prices for oil which are prevalent in the world today. The hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain said something to the effect that the government was moving rapidly, in a blundering way, in the direction of price and wage controls. This bill as it relates to oil pricing, export tax and compensation was before the Canadian people at the time of the July 8 general election. The government's policy on oil pricing was consistent before and during the election campaign, and it has been consistent since the election. I am not sure which side the hon. member was on in the debate that took place within the Progressive Conservative Party as it related to wage and price controls. However, I would not think any member of the official opposition would want to talk very loudly about blundering in respect of wage and price controls.
The hon. member seemed to be especially concerned about consultation in the establishment of prescribed prices for oil and gas. As I read the bill, part II, division I provides for this when it speaks about "mutually acceptable prices" between the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and the producer provinces. It goes on, in the second part of that division, to talk about reciprocal orders in council to implement these prescribed prices. It seems to me that this government has shown that consultation does not rest just at the official level or at the level of cabinet ministers, but extends right up to the first ministers of our country. This was amply demonstrated in the agreement on oil prices reached by the first ministers last March; also this week during the consultation on other important matters relating to our economy.
Let us consider this proposed legislation in somewhat broader perspective. The world energy economy is undergoing a traumatic adjustment process to a new set of economic and political realities. These are relatively unchartered waters, and bold and imaginative responses are required from governments, industry and individuals if we are to ease the transition to a new energy environment. Most members are aware of the many facets of this new environment, which include a quadrupling of international oil prices in less than one year; a correspondingly large transfer of wealth, about $100 billion, annually to a small number of oil exporting nations; Increases in demands for aid from the less developed parts of the world; the possibility that overseas oil supply could be disrupted at almost any time, for political reasons.
In response to this environment, most oil importing nations are seeking a more rational use of energy in an effort to reduce demand, and at the same time are endeavouring to encourage increased production from indigenous sources. If successful, both measures would, of course, serve to reduce dependence upon imported crude oil. At the same time, international financial institutions
are trying to devise arrangements to channel the greatly increased wealth of the oil exporting nations to imports of industrial goods, to develop and diversify the producing nations' economies, to aid for developing countries, and to international capital markets in an effort to ease the strain on the already precarious balance of payments positions of many oil importing nations. Unfortunately, efforts to reduce the high, worldwide rates of inflation-of which greatly increased oil prices is one contributing factor- have to date met with very little success.
Among the industrialized nations of the world, Canada is in a relatively favoured position in this new energy environment because of our self-sufficiency in petroleum. However, our resources, for the most part, are located in western Canada, while the large consumption centres are in eastern Canada, necessitating long distance transportation systems. In order to economize on the cost of moving oil to markets, it was advantageous to export some of our petroleum production to markets in the United States while importing oil from markets east of Ontario.
In 1973, petroleum accounted for approximately 5 per cent of the volume of Canada's merchandise exports. In 1974, as a result of higher export prices, it is expected that this proportion will increase to over 10 per cent. Imports of petroleum roughly balance our oil exports, resulting in no net balance of trade implications. However, since we are net exporters of natural gas, as gas increases in market value following oil prices we can expect a significant increase in export earnings of roughly $10 million annually for each cent per thousand cubic foot increase in the border price of gas.
Petroleum and gas are also very important commodities in interprovincial trade, and will probably amount to $2.5 billion in 1974. The Canadian energy economy, therefore, bears a similarity to the world energy economy: oil and gas in Canada are the most important sources of energy, accounting for almost 80 per cent of energy consumed; the oil and gas resources are located a considerable distance from major consuming centres, resulting in significant trade between producing and consuming regions; and the producing regions desire to use the wealth derived from the exploitation of their non-renewable resources to further diversify and industrialize their economies.
However, we must recognize that if Canadian oil prices were to track world oil prices, severe strains would be forced on our national economy similar to those now facing the world economy. For example, if domestic oil prices had not been held at several dollars a barrel below world prices, Canadians could be experiencing a rate of inflation perhaps 2 per cent higher, and fuel oil prices might be as much as 15 cents a gallon higher than current prices. In addition, severe financial imbalances could have arisen between our producing and consuming regions, which might have imposed serious strains on our confederation.
We recognize that oil and gas prices must increase from the low levels to which we have become accustomed, first, if producing provinces are to secure an equitable return for a non-renewable resource and, second, to encourage the development of our frontier oil and gas resources in

November 1, 1974

order to ensure sources of supply in the future. Third, they must increase in order to discourage the continuation of wasteful consuming practices in respect of our energy resources and, fourth, in recognition of the fact that Canada is an open trading nation who cannot isolate herself, for any extended period of time, from the international environment. We also recognize that prices should not be allowed to increase in such a way as to put our primary and secondary industries at a disadvantage in relation to their competitors, particularly in the United States where oil prices are lower than international levels.
Fortunately, Canada's unique position permits, us, within certain limits, to control our own destiny in regard to the development of oil, gas and other energy prices. Canadian consumers and industries can and will adjust to higher energy prices by, first, better insulation; second, smaller-engined automobiles; third, more efficient energy conversion equipment in factories; fourth, greater use of public transportation systems, and so on. But it takes time to effect many of these changes, It therefore appears prudent for Canada to follow a course of moderation in the transition to higher prices, thereby reducing the social costs and political strains associated with the necessary adjustment to the new world energy environment.
This principle was recognized and accepted by the first ministers last spring. It has been implemented in a manner which minimizes the financial burdens within the economy and cushions the impact on consumers, private and commercial, without ignoring the legitimate interests of the producing provinces. For example, revenues accruing to the Alberta treasury are expected to increase by nearly $1 billion over the level of oil and gas revenues received in the last fiscal year.
In my opinion, Bill C-32 is essential to implement the principles agreed to by the first ministers. Part II provides for an oil pricing agreement between producing and consuming interests in this country. The power to determine maximum oil prices by the federal government acting unilaterally would only be invoked as a last resort. Part III stipulates similar pricing provisions for natural gas. Part I of Bill C-32 will ensure that the difference between Canadian oil prices and the just and reasonable price for that oil in the export market will be appropriated by means of an export charge, while part IV will reduce the cost of imported oil to Canadian consumers so as to achieve oil pricing equality across the country.
Part IV would also provide for compensation of the additional transportation costs that might be incurred in moving western Canadian oil to eastern markets in the event of future disruption of our imported oil supplies. Part V of the bill will empower the minister to undertake certain administrative functions essential to an efficient and tidy management of the act. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I support the passage of Bill C-32 for the role it has to play in the development of sound energy policy, and the opportunity it affords Canadians to be masters of their own destiny during this difficult transition period.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING THE ADMINISTRATION OF INTERPROVINCIAL. EXPORT AND IMPORT TRADE IN PETROLEUM AND PETROLEUM PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is a treat for a member who has been in this House as long as I have to be able to look at such a pretty face when making a speech. If this is part of the women's liberation movement, then I am in favour of it.
Oil and Petroleum
As the previous speaker indicated when he began his remarks, this is a critical situation within our nation because there is a real and present danger to the world as a result of the events associated with the distribution of world energy resources, more especially in relation to oil. Because we are a fortunate nation with what appear to be more than adequate resources, both now and for the foreseeable future, our plight is possibly not as serious as that facing other parts of the world.
However, there is a serious situation because many of the known resources of oil and gas are located in one part of the nation and, as a result, the whole nation cannot readily secure any advantage from these resources. Therefore, somewhat complicated but acceptable solutions have been worked out. Up until now we have been exporting part of our resources to other parts of the world, while at the same time we have been importing the same amount from other parts of the world. Agreement to this sort of arrangement was not a problem for the nation until last year, when the world faced skyrocketing increases because of certain external actions taken mainly by the Arab oil producing nations. These increases were followed by a similar type of escalation in the cost of oil by the South American countries, one of our major sources of supply.
The solution to the problem, which is partly contained in this legislation so far as the federal government is concerned, is very complex and carries with it some serious complications from the strictly Canadian point of view. I say this because it will produce a great many altercations between the federal government and the provincial governments. These must be solved in a manner wherein both the parties, and the public in general, are protected. At the same time, we must not leave scars on the constitution which will be impossible to remove in future negotiations between the federal government and the governments of the provinces.
The speeches today have outlined, in a good deal of detail, some of the complications associated with this legislation, as well as some of the things that have already happened. Some of the things that have happened give every parliamentarian, whether he be associated with the federal parliament or one of the provincial legislatures, a great deal of concern for the nation. We are concerned about the nation being able to stay together in face of what appears to be, on the surface, in this legislation substantial intrusion by the federal authority into the provincial realm. One thing that amazes me is that federal politicians should be expressing almost greater concern about what is happening at the moment than is indicated by the provincial premiers. It almost seems that the provincial premiers are more anxious to let those who are feeling the brunt of the federal decision carry the burden, in the hope that it will not happen to them. But as the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) pointed out in his speech, what may be a problem for Alberta and Saskatchewan today could very easily be a problem for Ontario and Quebec tomorrow, and the day after that it could be a problem for Atlantic Canada.
So while I am rather hesitant to put forward my concern, as a federal politician, for some of the problems faced

November 1, 1974
Oil and Petroleum
by provincial governments, at the same time I feel it is absolutely necessary that I place before the minister some of my concerns, as a member of parliament from the Atlantic provinces, regarding what I anticipate may be a far greater problem in future because of what is now happening in my part of Canada. It is very obvious to me, and I am sure to the minister and to members from Atlantic Canada, that we are slowly but surely reaching the position where we will become one of the great oil and gas producers, not just of this nation but of the world. It could well be, as the result of strikes that have been announced in recent weeks, which I am sure will continue to be announced in the days ahead, that offshore Atlantic Canada holds the same kind of riches as those discovered in the North Sea.
As a result, it is imperative that a number of things be done by this government, including allowing the resources of the areas in question to flow to the provinces in which they are found, and to be under their jurisdiction as far as rights and benefits are concerned. This has not been the case up to now, and if this legislation is put into effect it may not be the case in the future. I think that in many ways this legislation poses threats to Atlantic Canada, just as it poses threats to the western provinces which are oil and gas producers at the moment. One thing that impressed me in the speech of the hon. member for Qu'ap-pelle-Moose Mountain and that of the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) was this: up to this moment, Alberta and Saskatchewan, in the main, have provided benefits out of the revenues obtained from their resources to the tune of $3 billion annually. They have done this in order to establish in Canada a single price for oil and gas.
Far too often during the past year the governments of those two provinces were made out to be gougers of the Canadian public, while in fact they have displayed generosity never before asked of a provincial government in providing their resources at a far lower price than could have been obtained under past arrangements. It is an extreme price for Saskatchewan to pay because-like most parts of Atlantic Canada-they are a have-not area and must value every dollar they can get their hands on, by whatever means available, in order to uplift the economy and improve and the lot of their people.
We, in Atlantic Canada, have a special interest because, although for a long time we have been one of the unfortunate parts of this nation, there are many indications, going well beyond the discovery of oil and gas off our shores, that we will become the power-house not just of the eastern Canadian seaboard but of the whole of North America, certainly the eastern part. We have established power resources associated with Brinco. We have the anticipated power developments associated with the Fundy tidal power, coupled with the move, now, by the government of New Brunswick into the nuclear power field. All this indicates that we shall certainly be a powerhouse for eastern Canada and the northeastern United States and, with a proper national system, we could be a power-house for the whole of Canada. Because of this we must look very carefully at any piece of federal legislation which in any way tries to take over what has been firmly established as provincial jurisdiction. I refer to jurisdiction over resources.

Yet, time after time the minister has made statements to the following effect: that it is of the utmost importance for the federal authority to be given firm control over our resources and the final say with regard to how our resources are to be developed and used. For instance, as recorded on page 914 of Hansard for October 31, 1974, the minister said:
We are ... affected by this change in the world situation and we wish to play a constructive role as a member of the international community while at the same time taking action to protect ourselves.
I have referred to the international action being taken. In the bill before us this afternoon we are dealing with domestic action contemplated to protect ourselves in this new situation. Bill C-32, the Petroleum Administration Act, is intended to provide the federal government with a statutory basis for the management, necessary in the interests of all Canadians, of important areas of international and interprovincial trade in petroleum and natural gas. Enactment of the legislation is essential if the government is to have the means to continue to guide the Canadian energy economy safely in the present turbulent global oil environment.
In other words the minister says that because the world is turbulent, the government will assume full jurisdiction over our resources, even though such jurisdiction from the constitutional and legal point of view has been vested in the provinces.
The minister went on to say:
-perhaps the central feature of our oil and energy policy relates to the pricing of domestic crude oil.
Then he said that the department will continue to refine and develop assessments of the net price necessary to "attract the capital trained manpower and technology" which will be needed if our energy resources are to be developed. This, according to the minister, will "provide the supply we will need in the future." In other words the government will determine what the supply is to be. The minister went on to say:
The social aspect consists primarily in finding a position of equity between the needs and interests of consuming and producing provinces in relation to the return which is necessary to justify the exploitation of this non-renewable resource.
The minister is suggesting that it is equitable to allow Alberta and Saskatchewan, our major oil producing provinces, to contribute between $2.9 billion and $3 billion to this country. The government is being very generous. I wonder how long the governments of Alberta and Saskatchewan will think this state of affairs equitable. How long will the people of those provinces be willing, in the name of equity, to provide this kind of money from their treasuries? Nova Scotia may think this state of affairs equitable, as will Ontario. The question is: will the people of Saskatchewan or Alberta for very much longer go along with this idea of equity? What is happening may be necessary in the short-run in order to protect our consumers, but we should not expect one part of the country to support another part for very long, especially as we are dealing in non-renewable resources for which there is no tomorrow, there being no replacement for them.
Let me now speak of off-shore resources. For a long time we have tried to resolve a recognizable problem regarding jurisdiction over off-shore resources. Agreements of one sort and another have been negotiated over the years. In this connection may I refer to an article in the "Journal of
November 1, 1974

Canadian Studies" written by Hal Mills, who said on page
57:
The offshore mineral rights dispute has been an overt one for over nine years, and has gone through five major stages, with an acceptable solution still to emerge. The foregoing history of the controversy leaves little doubt as to the prevalence of stages of deadlock, as well as the ill-will and resentment engendered throughout. If the total complex of federal-provincial relations is to be of a continuing and effective nature, one must expect individual conflicts, such as the offshore mineral rights dispute, to be resolved with a maximum of speed and a minimum loss of goodwill between participants at both levels of government.
The dispute continues, without sign of resolution. Indeed only the Premier of Newfoundland seems willing to stand firm and fast in his belief that his province owns the right to all resources offshore Newfoundland. Similarly, I and my leader believe that Nova Scotia has the right to 100 per cent of the benefits associated with the resources off our shores. The same may be said of all five eastern provinces. Yet there is no indication that the government is willing to do today more than it was willing to do nine years ago, and concede to the peoples of the areas concerned the right of offshore resources and the benefits associated with their development.
There is a real danger that we cannot get our resources developed because the government will determine the price of our resources, a price which may be far below that available internationally. As a result, prospects for exploration and development will go out of the window. Machinery for development is already moving to other parts of the world where economic prospects are better than in this country. So long as we depend on money, those engaged in exploration will go where they can make most of it.
The hon. member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse) has handed me a recent copy of Financial Post which contains this headline: "Oil-sands withdrawal comes as a bombshell." I point out that "bombshell" refers to Shell Oil Company. The text says that the Shell Oil Company's decision to withdraw from its 50 per cent holding in Shell's Athabasca oil sands project hit Calgary like a bombshell last week. I can only say that if the government continues on its present course we shall see many such statements. We are bound to see money for exploration leaving this country and heading for the North Sea, the South Pacific, as well as other places.
Atlantic Canada needs massive development if its people are to have some prospect of the sort of life which was anticipated would be theirs when they became part of this nation in 1867. This development has not taken place, and we have less chance every day that the government holds off, or because of this or that action that has been taken to eliminate this or that opportunity for us. There is no doubt that the rich get richer and the poor get poorer. That seems to have been the policy of the government since it has taken office.
In the days of the Diefenbaker administration we had one policy after another which enhanced the opportunities of our people. It gave us at least a hope of catching up with the rest of the nation. However, those actions have been
Oil and Petroleum
destroyed on the altar of expediency to benefit the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, especially Quebec.
It is very difficult for our people to look at confederation today and feel they have an even chance or an even break. That opportunity is just not there. If Fundy tidal power were located in Ontario or Quebec, it would have been developed 20 years ago. We are still waiting. We are waiting either for translators or someone else to tell us that the government is going to order another study, or do something else, before it can take a serious look to see whether something can be done about this project.
The people of Atlantic Canada are in the same boat with regard to offshore resources. We have asked for equity, justice, and a right under the constitution. We asked the government to do as much for us as was done for other areas of this nation when they were allowed to increase their boundaries and pick up rich resource land. The government says it wants to talk more. It does not believe we have any more right to those resources than anyone else in Canada. That could be true if every other part of Canada had been treated the same since the beginning, but that is not the case. Other parts of this nation were allowed to expand their boundaries. We believe we have a right to expand ours.
If Nova Scotia is going to extend its boundaries they will have to be extended under the sea because there is no more land available on top of the sea. Our party has recognized that province's right and our obligation. We recognize the fact that we should assist Atlantic Canada, not with half-baked schemes produced in ivory towers in Ottawa, but with development of resources that exist in our area to give our people equal opportunity. I am fearful that if the government moves in with the big grab that is associated with this legislation, takes the power away from the provinces and takes the resources or control of them away, then we in Atlantic Canada will have little hope for the future. Indeed we will have to accept the fact that we are going to be second-class citizens for as long as this government holds office.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING THE ADMINISTRATION OF INTERPROVINCIAL. EXPORT AND IMPORT TRADE IN PETROLEUM AND PETROLEUM PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to speak on Bill C-32 for at least the second time. A similar bill was dealt with in this House and in committee last April. However, an election and other things intervened.
This is an important bill because it puts together some of the essential components of a national energy policy. I am referring to a single, equitable, reasonable price across Canada.
I find it very difficult to follow the reasoning of the hon. member for Cumberland-Colchester North (Mr. Coates). He talked about the hardships of the eastern provinces, which I fully understand. However, this bill in effect sets a fair price of $6.50 a barrel for oil, plus transportation, for all of Canada.

speechtext: Nonsense.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING THE ADMINISTRATION OF INTERPROVINCIAL. EXPORT AND IMPORT TRADE IN PETROLEUM AND PETROLEUM PRODUCTS
speechtext:
It is about $4 or $5 cheaper than the world price. Eastern Canada is traditionally served by the world market. This is a way of subsidizing eastern Canadians and of having a considerably lower price in the maritimes.

November 1, 1974
Oil and Petroleum
This bill, which secures this single, fair, equitable price was fought out between the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the premiers of the provinces. I think the price of $6.50 is fair. I do not feel the federal government could go beyond that price. If more demands had been made and, if it had been impossible to agree to something more than this, we would have had to go to a national marketing board or something of that nature.
The have provinces, in terms of oil and natural gas, have made some concessions in connection with this bill. With some of these concessions there has to be a quid pro quo, particularly in the area of transportation. There must be a complete reworking of our transportation policy which will favour areas other than Toronto, Montreal and Ottawa. That is part and parcel of the quid pro quo for this price which is certainly $4 or $5 below the price on the world market.
There are three major areas in terms of an energy policy for this country that we must consider. There is the single, equitable, reasonable, fair price, something I feel this bill achieves. The second is that there be a larger Canadian component, with greater Canadian ownership of our resources. This is something we must work at, Mr. Speaker. There will soon be some action on this front with the setting up of the Canadian Petroleum Corporation. The third, and perhaps the most important, is having a secure supply of all forms of energy. Canadians need to be basically self sufficient and have a secure energy supply for a long period of time. In this whole notion of secure supply there must be some kind of levelling of demand in order to equate supply and demand. We cannot always have supply chasing demand.
I wish to deal with some of the long-term problems in terms of oil and gas, our energy requirements, and some concerns I have about achieving a secure supply, pricing and everything else that goes along with it. If we are to believe those who speak with authority in this energy field, we have to accept the fact that Canada is going to require investments of up to $100 billion in the next 10 to 15 years.
It is estimated the James Bay project will cost something in the order of $12 billion. There is an application for a Mackenzie Valley gas pipeline that will cost $6 billion plus. There is the possibility of a Mackenzie Valley oil pipeline. The United States government has been and is talking about this. It will cost between $8 billion and $10 billion. Massive investment will be required in the Athabasca tar sands to maintain a supply situation in oil. Each plant would cost about $1.5 billion, and anywhere from 15 to 20 Of these plants would be needed in operation by the end of the eighties. So we are talking here about another $30 billion or $40 billion; the estimates I have seen could add up to around $100 billion.
I am concerned when I hear the press talk, rather lightly, about the desirability of establishing another nuclear enrichment plant. What would be the cost? Around $2 billion? This is not taking account of the extra billion dollars or two billion dollars required to provide the necessary 2,000 megawatts of power. We must consider the effect of these investments. How great are they to be, and

what distortion effects can be expected from them? There are three areas of danger, and I am not dealing now with the environment, the effect upon native peoples, and so on, important as these aspects are.
First, we should consider the effect upon capital flow itself. What would be the effect upon our economy and upon our currency of a massive capital flow from the United States or from Japan? If the capital comes mainly from sources within Canada, what would be the effect in terms of our ability to accomplish other tasks?
Specifically, if we pursue the James Bay project at a cost of $12 billion and simultaneously the Mackenzie Valley oil pipeline scheme at a cost of $8 billion, where will the bucks come from to build houses? We have to take into account the effect on the Canadian dollar itself. What happens to the pulp and paper industry if the value of the Canadian dollar is forced upward by a massive inflow of capital? I come from the city of Thunder Bay, which is tremendously dependent upon sales of pulp and paper and is greatly concerned about markets for this product.
We should also be concerned about the consequences of selling our energy. If Japan or the United States buy increasing supplies of our energy will they be able to purchase, in addition, manufactured goods which we are capable of supplying? Or do we become more and more hewers of water?

speechtext:
I put the two, water and wood, together. At the rate we are going we will soon not have any wood left.
I am really concerned about this distortion effect. Those responsible for policy should look at our long range objectives in two ways. First, I do not think we can continue to respond affirmatively to requests for this project or that project. The time has come for decisions to be taken as between alternative projects. For example, is the polar pipeline a more sensible approach, or should some other project be preferred? Are there inter-modal facets which ought to be considered?
When we are considering the supply of gas, should we also be considering coal gasification? I believe we should. People to whom I have spoken, people who know something about these things, believe there is a great possibility here, and that the technology is not very far off. I believe we must make a choice between the various projects open to us. If we seek to do all of them at once I believe other important sectors of the economy will be neglected. I think, too, the provinces must realize that they, too, cannot enter upon projects of this scale without some kind of general consensus being reached. For example, aside from its effects on the native people, how far should the James Bay project go? It looks as though James Bay power will be very expensive; a nuclear alternative
November 1, 1974

would be a great deal cheaper, it seems to me, judging from the figures I have been able to find.
Even more important is the whole subject of energy conservation. We see demand curves which follow an extremely steep slope. The supply curves for almost all the energy commodities which one can think of, cross at some point in the eighties. At some point we shall be bound to reduce the slope of these demand curves. Sustained growth in the energy area cannot be maintained along present lines. Thus it seems to me that one of the main components of the supply situation is our success in getting the demand curve to level off so that supplies may, at least, be secure.
I should like to discuss one or two possibilities in the field of conservation. First, I should like to see studies conducted to show, as I am sure they would, that money spent on conservation would result, dollar for dollar, in more energy than money spent on exploration and other development. Those who are concerned with conservation should be placing the results of such studies before us.
One area which should be examined closely is that of transportation. There is no question that there is a great demand for a satisfactory public transportation system, something which would in itself tend to conserve energy. From the point of view of conserving energy, ground transport is vastly more efficient than transport by air- the factor is something like ten to one. This is particularly the case when short journeys are made, because most of the energy used by an aircraft is used in getting the plane up to 25,000 feet.
It seems to me we ought to move rapidly to establish better ground transportation facilities between Ottawa, Toronto and Montreal, large communities which are relatively close together. My own feeling is that projects such as the Pickering airport might not be needed if we adopt improved ground transportation as an alternative to air travel.
We live in a country which, in the past, has fortunately been blessed with very cheap energy. We find energy more costly today, it is becoming scarce, and we should begin to think of building our houses in such a way as to conserve a great deal more energy. For example, we could use solar experiments, locating our houses to benefit from solar heat. Different methods of insulating are called for also. These are two aspects that we could explore, but it is extremely important that we do everything we can to flatten out the demand curve.
Then we should insist that the automobile manufacturers in this country produce automobiles that will get a minimum of 20 miles to the gallon. No car should be built today that does not get that mileage. Mention was made in the budget of taxing large cars. I think the tax should be contingent upon mileage. If a car can deliver only 12 miles to the gallon and is certified as such, a heavy tax should be placed on the car. We must make every effort to get cars with good gasoline mileage.
I think that if time, effort and money are spent on conservation we will avoid some of the massive problems that will confront us if we decide within the next ten years to commence huge projects costing $100 million. As I
Oil and Petroleum
have said, if we pursue the idea of massive energy investment and our energy growth continues in the way it is today, then we will create tremendous distortions in our economy, indeed in our whole way of life.
Therefore, I suggest we look at these individual items, decide which are the important ones, and develop priorities. These priorities must be national in scope; it must not be a case of one province wanting to do one thing and another province wanting to do another. Secondly, we should spend a lot of money to convince all Canadians, through advertising and in any other way, that some kind of slight modification of our lifestyle is going to be required if we are to continue living in harmony with our environment in this country.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING THE ADMINISTRATION OF INTERPROVINCIAL. EXPORT AND IMPORT TRADE IN PETROLEUM AND PETROLEUM PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bill before us is, in essence, a resurrection of the petroleum administration bill of the last parliament, and to the extent that the oil omnibus bill duplicates its predecessor, it also inherits its faults. To the extent that additions have been made, the government has simply gone further in its assault on provincial jurisdiction over natural resources. The new measures concerning gas pricing do nothing to mitigate the war of nerves being waged between Alberta and Ottawa. The overt refusal to consult and to conduct serious negotiations with the energy producing provinces serves only to further alienate them and to drive a negotiated solution further out of reach.
This legislation further reflects the Liberal government's propensity to increase its power ambit under the guise of emergency powers, by enacting measures to be used "in case an agreement cannot be reached". More specifically, what is offered here is legislation that would give the government the unilateral power to set natural gas and oil prices nationally, but outside the borders of the provinces where the energy is being produced.
Let me say to the minister through you, Mr. Speaker, that to ensure that domestic natural gas prices do not jump drastically next fall, but increase in stages over a reasonable time frame to price levels competitive with the domestic oil price, seems to be a rational objective. But the methods herein proposed are draconian. I believe strongly, and our party has always stated, that an agreement on what constitutes a fair price should be arrived at by the process of negotiation, and only then should we attempt to stage increases over a reasonable period of time to ease the impact on Canadian consumers. There has been no indication that any let alone all ten provinces have agreed with Bill C-32's provisions.
The minister admits that Alberta has already warned that it would oppose any federal government action to exercise jurisdiction over natural gas pricing, and the signals are clearly out that a further round of charges, counter-charges and confrontation between the governments involved will ensue, leaving a further legacy of bitterness and sense of alienation in its wake.
The minister has attempted to placate the voices of opposition members by pointing out that if Ottawa and the provinces are able to agree to a staged increase over the next few years, to cushion domestic consumers, the federal legislation on gas pricing would not have to be used. In fact, however, domestic gas prices are scheduled

November 1, 1974
Oil and Petroleum
to jump 22 cents a thousand cubic feet today under new gas rates approved by the National Energy Board last week. Furthermore, under Alberta law gas selling prices are scheduled to be revalued again next year.
Instead of waiting until after further discussions with Alberta on the matter, which I understand are scheduled for November 12, the minister wants the Commons to approve his legislation and grant him these extensive powers at once. How can meaningful, good faith negotiations take place when the minister has in advance armed himself with the power to legislate an agreement? In addition to this objectionable aspect, the proposed legislation also allows the federal government to determine how extra revenues from increased gas prices should be distributed between producer, transmission companies and governments.
It is not an overstatement to say that this bill is an assertion of almost total authority and control over petroleum resource development in Canada, and as such flies in the face of our constitution and historical provincial prerogatives.
On the whole question of petroleum pricing I would commend to the minister for his serious consideration an observation made by C. E. S. Fraser in an article on energy published in the Queen's Quarterly last summer. He said:
Over the long run, it is unlikely that Canada can, and undesirable that Canada should, remain an isolated oasis of cheap petroleum.
Proper analysis suggests that oil and gas are not so cheap or so plentiful in Canada as some politicians appear to believe.
The real value of Canadian petroleum supplies is that they can stabilize short-term fluctuations of supply and cost, and in so doing reduce the harmful effects of the inevitable but painful readjustments of world energy industries during the next half century.
But, Mr. Speaker, important as the constitutional questions raised by this legislation are-and they are of fundamental importance-I wish to discuss another matter of even greater concern to the people of Canada, namely, the question of security of supply.
Two years ago Canada possessed a domestic petroleum industrial organization in which she could take great pride, an industry comprising over 300 separate producing companies and which, in the preceding 20 or so years, had grown and developed from relative insignificance to a threshold of strength and competence which rendered it able to operate in competition throughout the world. Plans were afoot in terms of additional development of our domestic petroleum resources, including the tar sands and the transportation facilities incidental to these, that would have assured the Canadian consumer of uninterrupted supplies of oil and natural gas for decades to come. The task was neither easy nor cheap in terms of the capital required, but the goal was attainable.
What is the situation today? Recently released statistics on drilling and exploration activity in Canada are cause for real concern. I suggest with all sincerity to the minister that he is over-sanguine in his response to this situation and these trends which, if not reversed, will create in five or ten years in Canada the same kinds of supply shortfalls now being experienced by our neighbour to the south, but with an impact on our society, if only by reason of geography, far more serious in nature.

During the next 20 or 30 years and beyond, the problem in Canadian petroleum policy, at least as much as keeping prices or the federal-provincial distribution of revenues down, will be to mobilize the investment and resources needed to develop our reserves. But instead western Canada's drilling activity is experiencing a serious decline, brought about by the sense of doubt, uncertainty and insecurity felt by the Canadian petroleum industry as a result of the moves and countermoves of federal and provincial governments in the last 18 months or so.
The number of wells completed during the first nine months this year was almost 8 per cent below the same 1973 period, and with the continuing emphasis on shallow gas drilling footage was down 10 per cent. With the likelihood of this trend continuing into the final three months, the tally for 1974 will be very close to 3,900 wells completed and 13.9 million feet of hole drilled, compared with 4,390 wells and 15.9 million feet of hole last year, a level of activity only slightly above the level of 1972.
Preliminary statistics compiled to the end of September indicate a total of 2,967 exploratory and development wells were completed in western Canada, including the Arctic, for a decrease of 245 from the first three-quarters of 1973, while footage was off 1.2 million feet to 10.6 million feet. This disappointing decrease in activity was reflected in the average active rig count which fell to 155 units for the nine months, with a drop of 12 per cent from 174 rigs working last year. This represents a utilization of only 48 per cent of the 322 rigs available for work.
The number of rigs working in eastern Canada, Quebec, the Atlantic provinces and offshore averaged four compared with six last year. But of even more concern is the number of rigs being moved to the United States and Alaska, and in most instances the rigs are of deep hole capacity. A total of 39 drilling rigs has been taken out of Canada this year to work in the United States and overseas, together with about 250 experienced, competent and trained personnel.
While various reasons and explanations are offered for this exodus, it is my view, shared I believe by most knowledgeable people in this area, that the uncertainties over our taxation and energy policies in Canada, aggravated by the ongoing intergovernmental squabbling between governments on energy issues, is the main motivation for this seriously disturbing trend in our domestic petroleum industry.
The decrease in wildcat drilling was a disappointing 16 per cent, with 261 fewer tests for a total of 1,386, while the footage decline amounted to 12 per cent, with a drop of 778,600 feet to 5.7 million feet. A total of 122 oil wells were brought in, down from 147, while gas finds decreased by 18 per cent to 476, and abandoned holes were 130 less at 788.
There were 2,553 wells licensed in Alberta during the first nine months compared with 2,634 last year, and almost 80 per cent were located east of the fifth meridian, with development wells outnumbering exploratory tests 2.5 to 1.
In Saskatchewan the situation is even more alarming. The number of wells drilled in the first nine months totalled 220, compared with 410 a year ago, while footage
November 1, 1974

was cut almost in half to 530,000 feet against more than one million feet in 1973. There were 142 wildcats completed, 57 less than a year ago, accompanied by a 38 per cent decline in footage to 337,200 feet. Only 78 field wells were completed, 142 less than a year ago, with footage off 65 per cent.
The drop reflects the industry's reaction to the political initiatives undertaken by Premier Blakeney's government, with most of the ongoing drilling involving commitment wells. It is essential that the energy climate of Canada be stabilized if we are to again enjoy the benefits of a dynamic and vital domestic petroleum industry which, if given the opportunity, is capable of providing our country with the energy reserves required to maintain our place in the industrial world in which we live.
The suggestion that federal or provincial governments, by direct intervention and investment in the petroleum industry will contribute in a significant way to Canada's over-all energy position is, in my view, erroneous, and I am supported in that view by the policy document of the minister's own department published last year.
The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) said Canadians should own and control their own resources. The Canadian people already own, either at the provincial or federal level, virtually all the oil and gas lands in this country and furthermore, the government possesses the power to regulate the terms of participation in development by private industry and to stipulate royalty rates and levels of taxation to be imposed on income produced therefrom.
I am at a loss to understand what significant benefits can be expected from the creation of a so-called national petroleum corporation in this country. On the other hand I am only too well aware of the negative factors involved, including discouragement of the private sector, wasteful dispersal of resources and talents already in short supply, and the enlargement of the bureaucratic establishment already overly large.
It would make far more sense, and be of greater ultimate benefit to the Canadian people for the federal government as an alternative to deploy the assets it intends to commit to the national petroleum corporation, to the research and development required to make available alternative renewable energy resources, a field in which the government's performance to date is, by comparison with other nations, lamentable.
The Montreal pipeline extension is another example of an over-complacent attitude on the part of the minister with respect to guaranteeing Canadians adequate supplies of domestic oil. I do not often agree with the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands on energy policy, but I share his view that the pipeline extension project should be undertaken as an instrument of national security with a serious sense of urgency and purpose now lacking, and if that requires, as it likely will because of the economics of the situation, government involvement or ownership, so be it.
I go further and suggest to the minister that he seriously study the possible benefits in terms of emergency supply capability of creating under public ownership facilities for the storage of a 60-day reserve supply of oil in eastern
Oil and Petroleum
Canada. This type of initiative is being undertaken by the governments of other industrialized countries on a much larger scale, notably Japan, and is a policy option which I suggest deserves serious examination.
In conclusion I repeat my opposition to the elements in this legislation creating a unilateral price fixing mechanism over petroleum and natural gas. I underline my concern regarding long-term security of supply in this country in light of the demoralized condition of the industry, and I urge immediate federal government initiatives to effect the construction of the Montreal pipeline extension to ensure our capability to move 250,000 barrels of oil or more a day into eastern Canada, thereby reducing its dependence on foreign supplies.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING THE ADMINISTRATION OF INTERPROVINCIAL. EXPORT AND IMPORT TRADE IN PETROLEUM AND PETROLEUM PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, this is a great opportunity for one of those five or ten minute speeches which comes before you see the clock. Therefore, I think I should say something about what has impressed me.
In listening to the debate to this point I was impressed by the sort of conciliatory tone of many of the members from western Canada. This is something very heartening to me, being from Ontario, as up until very recently whenever this subject of energy has arisen there was an obvious bitterness on the part of western members in the sense that they were being asked, on behalf of their provinces, to take less in the way of revenue than they felt they were entitled to receive.
As a person from Ontario, recognizing the substantial benefit we in Ontario are receiving because of the lower price at which we are able to obtain energy supplies from western Canada, I want to thank the people of western Canada. I appreciate that, and I think it is a good thing in our confederation that this kind of attitude prevails, once the quarrelling and argument are toned down.
It is unnecessary to remind people from western Canada that Ontario for a long time, in fact for 11 years under the national oil policy, was prepared to pay higher prices for energy in recognition of the fact that we needed to develop energy supplies and sources in western Canada. There was not very much grumbling about that. That was an expensive program for the rest of Canada. We have various figures in this regard, including those of the National Energy Board, which would indicate a cost to consumers in Canada of $500 million over the 11-year period. My calculations would show that it is much greater, something closer to $500 million a year, in other words 11 times greater, but I do not want to get into any arguments on that ground. I am simply saying this conciliatory tone is really something that fills me with pleasure.
There are understandable differences. People who have the resources want as much for those resources as possible, and the consuming parts of Canada think they should have those resources at as low a cost as possible. These differences are being resolved. We are engaged in this kind of negotiation.
While listening to the hon. member for Cumberland-Colchester North (Mr. Coates) I wondered whether he was adopting the kind of arrangement that is developing

November 1, 1974
Canada Pension Plan
in Scotland, where suddenly there is a new militancy in an area which has the prospect of oil and gas discoveries. Each part of Canada at one time or another either contributes or takes from the general pool of our society. I think it would be sad if, with the prospect of wealth, some part of Canada should forget that at other times it was on the other end of the equation. I sincerely hope there will be substantial discoveries on the east coast because any discoveries in the long run serve to enhance the future of this country and enable us to be a more affluent and self-serving country than otherwise might be the case.
It seems to me that in the future, if not now, we must move toward public ownership of our energy supplies. When I say this in respect of energy supplies I believe it to be important, because we should have that kind of ownership in order to have a rational allocation of energy. This includes gas, oil, coal, nuclear energy and hydro energy. Some of these are already under public ownership. Most of hydro is under public ownership and most nuclear energy in Canada is under public ownership, but not all. It is important that our energy supplies be under public ownership for the future of our country.
I am not making a general statement that public ownership is always better than private ownership because, in many ways, I have never been a strong proponent of public ownership. I think there are many areas where it is not a satisfactory answer. However, in the field of energy, because of the complexities and because of the importance of this field to the future of a country, there are strong arguments which can be made in favour of public ownership.
I understand, Mr. Speaker, that it is the wish of the House to move to another item, so may I move the adjournment of this debate.
