subsubtopic: BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT, 1867 AMENDMENT TO LIMIT TENURE OF SENATORS
speechtext:
that Bill C-207, to amend the British North America Act, 1867 (tenure of place of Senators), be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is always a pleasure to rise in this House on a Friday afternoon when there is a cozy atmosphere. One sometimes feels we should bring a picnic lunch, spread a cloth in the middle of the aisle, and pass away the remaining hours of our legislative week.
I am speaking today on behalf of my private member's bill, Bill C-207, to amend the British North America Act in respect of tenure of place of senators. This bill is part of a two-bill parley. It originated as a single bill to amend the Senate, but I was informed by the legal advisor that this suggested reform must take the form of two bills. In order to understand Bill C-207 it may be necessary for me occasionally to mention Bill C-261, to amend the British
November 1, 1974

North America Act in respect of the appointment of senators.
I think there has been a fairly widespread desire, from the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on down, that something must be done with regard to Senate reform. Perhaps first we should look at the reasons for Senate reform. The Senate was instituted in our parliamentary system for two main reasons: first, to give sober second thought to legislation and, second, to represent regions from which the senators were appointed, on a provincial basis. It is in the dereliction of these basic purposes that the Senate has fallen to its present low state. It must be reformed or one day soon the will of the people, as expressed here by the peoples' representatives, will be to do away with the Senate. Let us attempt to reform it. If the reforms do not make it viable then we will have to come to what Hitler referred to as the solution when he was speaking, of course, in another context.
Two recent events may point out how far the Senate has strayed from its original purpose. First I should like to remind hon. members, particularly new members, that last winter in the twenty-ninth Parliament the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang) introduced a bill commonly known as the wiretap bill. This bill was amended in committee. The amendments were voted on in this chamber. Some amendments carried, and some did not. Then the bill as amended was given third reading by the Commons and sent to the Senate.
One amendment was not attractive to the Minister of Justice. It must be borne in mind that it had been accepted by the majority of members of parliament here assembled. The Senate at that item, being more mindful of its party affiliation than of its duty, attempted to have the legislation re-amended to subordinate the will of the Commons to the will of the minister. The Senate amendment received the treatment it deserved. The bill was passed according to the wishes of the elected representatives and not the wishes of the appointed senators expressing their life-long gratitude to the government.
The second deleterious occurrence concerning the Senate was the use by the Liberal Party of the Senate in the recent election. We have become accustomed to the appointments to the Senate by successive prime ministers having a strong, perhaps overwhelming, smell of political reward, of payment for services rendered. But recently a new tendency has slipped in. Some Senators no longer make any pretence at impartiality and consider that it is their duty to support the party that appointed them, until death do them part.
I should like to read a few notes on some of the Senators of whom I am speaking. The national campaign headquarters of the Liberal Party listed Senator Keith Davey as the Campaign co-chairman. In speaking of Senator Davey I might read a news item from the Toronto Star of June 19, 1974, which goes as follows:
Federal executives responsible for preparing government announcements during the July 8 election campaign period have been ordered to clear all statements with Liberal campaign co-chairman, Senator Keith Davey...
A memo to that effect was sent to all ministerial executive assistants by Joyce Fairbairn, legislative assistant to Prime Minister Pierre
Senate Reform
Trudeau. The memo, however, has been circulated through government departments as well.
Purpose of the screening is to ensure that all announcements "receive maximum publicity through proper timing and presentation", the memo says.
Announcements and ministerial statements are to be sent to the Prime Minister's office "at least one week in advance".
"Senator Keith Davey will then judge the timing which would produce the maximum result", the memo says.
"Announcements should not be scheduled until his judgment is given". The "not" is underlined.
What relationship does such an activity bear to the original purpose of the Senate to give sober second thought to legislation, and to represent the regions from which the Senators are appointed? None whatsoever. It is this kind of activity that has brought disrepute to the Senate.

subsubtopic: BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT, 1867 AMENDMENT TO LIMIT TENURE OF SENATORS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT, 1867 AMENDMENT TO LIMIT TENURE OF SENATORS
speechtext:
Let me go on with the list of the national campaign headquarters of the Liberal Party. There is Senator Gildas Molgat listed as the president of the Liberal Party, Senator R. J. Perrault as campaign chairman for British Columbia, Senator Earl Hastings as chairman for Alberta, Senator Jean-Pierre Cote as chairman for Quebec, and Senator Lome Bonnell as Chairman for Prince Edward Island. Among those actively involved are John Aird of Toronto, Sidney Buckwold of Saskatoon, Douglas Everett of Winnipeg, Louis-Philippe Gelinas and Louis Giguere of Montreal, Harry Hays of Calgary, Dan Riley of Saint John, Irvine Barrow of Halifax, and George van Roggen of Vancouver. This group have done more to bring disrepute to and to misconstrue and misinterpret the role of the Senate than any group in recent history.
It is pretty clear that the Prime Minister should set about reforming the Senate. But, it is his belief that it is much better to have the taxpayers of Canada providing the dollars to operate his party than to take from the party chests. I should like to read from the Senate Hansard to show you what Senator Godfrey's impression is of his role. This is what he had to say:
I am, and have been since the fall of 1968, the chairman of the finance and treasury committees of the Liberal Party of Canada, and in that capacity I have the overall responsibility for raising the funds for the federal Liberal Party, not only at election time but also to maintain its activities between elections.
The Senate needs reform; nothing could be more clear. It is an absolute necessity that it be reformed quickly or it will be too late.
I should like to say that there are different groups of senators. There is the group I just listed, and there is the other kind, those who enchance upper chamber and Canadian politics by their presence. Although I admit to lack of detailed knowledge of the personalities and records of senators, I must say that in my short time in federal politics I have noticed Senator Cameron, Senator David Croll, Senator Forsey, Senator Goldenburg, Senator Gro-sart, Senator Lamontagne, Senator Manning, Senator O'Leary, Senator Belisle and Senator Yuzyk.
These gentleman do not look upon the Senate as a place in which to express their lifelong loyalty to one party or another. They look upon their responsibilities in a mature way and in the national sense. I tell you that it is only the

November 1, 1974
Senate Reform
achievement of these senators that convinces me that we should attempt to reform that body rather than follow the route prescribed by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). It is because of the work of the second group of senators that I have gone to considerable effort to prepare the two bills, Bill C-207 and Bill C-261.
Bill C-261 would provide a new method of selecting senators bases upon party standings in the House of Commons on January 1 of each year. The then existing vacancies could be allocated on a pro-rated basis among the parties, determined finally by the party leaders. The Governor General could announce the appointments. This would mean that the Senate membership would eventually bear some relationship to the desires of the Canadian people as expressed every four years at election time.
Bill C-207, the one with which we are dealing today, is a bill that has to do with the tenure of appointment. I put in both of these bills a year ago, but I did not win in the draw. In consequence, they were not heard. I put them in again and now have the opportunity to speak on one bill only.
The key words in Bill C-207 are:
A Senator who is summoned to the Senate after the coming into force of this subsection-
That means of course that it will not apply to any existing senators.
-shall, subject to this Act, hold his place in the Senate until he attains the age of seventy-five years or for a period not to exceed ten years, whichever occurs first.
It is not by accident that it say "ten years". Last year it said fifteen years, and this year, on October 2, the Prime Minister of Canada said that he had two reforms in mind for the Senate.
... First, we should limit the duration of senatorial appointments to a certain number of years, seven, for instance, with the option of reappointing senators when they have well served their country.
He is the Prime Minister and I am just an ordinary member, so I thought I would meet him somewhat more than halfway, that I would come down from fifteen to ten, and he could meet me and come up from seven to ten.
I am sure that hon. members opposite will agree that the bill complied closely enough with the Prime Minister's wishes, and therefore they will give it speedy passage later this afternoon and send it to committee.
With regard to the last portion of the sentence uttered by the Prime Minister, in which he wanted the option of reappointing senators when they have well served their country, let me say that this would destroy the purpose of any Senate reform if that option were vested in the Prime Minister. It would make people ask: how did senator X do in the last election? If he did not pull his weight for the party, he would not be reappointed and, if he worked hard, he would be reappointed. This would put the Senate even more under the control of the party in power.
I do not wish to insinuate that there is a great deal of difference between the parties in this respect. The difficulty in some regards is that one party has been in power a great deal of time lately in our country. I do not think that we are all saints and they are all sinners. I think the difference lies in the legislation power that is given to the party in charge, the party that is temporarily forming the

government, to abuse parliament by these types of appointments and employment of senators.
Finally, allow me to quote from the Senate Hansard for Tuesday, March 13, 1973. I shall quote the remarks of Senator Croll who suggested 12 points for Senate reform. I commend the speeches recorded in the Senate Hansard; invariably one finds extraordinarily good speeches, well researched and well constructed. I assure you it is easier to read a well constructed speech than to make one.
Senator Croll brought forward a 12-point plan for Senate reform in the seventies. He suggested, as reported at page 322, that the present absolute veto power of the Senate over all legislation should be reduced to a suspensive veto. I am glad that the Prime Minister agreed with the Senator in his speech of October 2, from which I quoted.
I do not agree with Senator Croll's suggested distribution of Senators. Once again he suggested the appointment of too many senators from this part of the world, and shortchanged western Canada, particularly British Columbia.
The third point must be considered in conjunction with the fourth. He, Senator Croll, suggested that the supporters of any one political party should not comprise more than two-thirds of the Senate at any one time, and that Canadian constitution should be amended as soon as possible to ensure this result.
Senator Croll went on to say:
The Senate is too heavily weighted on one side, and this is not good for the Senate. It is not good for democracy ... Good opposition makes for good government.
His next point was:
The government leader in the Senate should not be a member of the Cabinet.
The leader has to be our man. He is not, and it is time that we cut the umbilical cord with the House of Commons.
The Senator ended by saying:
It seems to me that there are only two options open-Senate reform or Senate abolition. It is a clear case of reform or perish.
I could not agree more with what Senator Croll said in his fine speech.

subsubtopic: BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT, 1867 AMENDMENT TO LIMIT TENURE OF SENATORS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, this is the first opportunity I have had to speak to the House. Therefore I would formally like to congratulate you on your appointment. I know in the very short time of this parliament that you and your colleagues have distinguished yourselves in the performance of your responsible duties.
I am very glad to participate today in this most academic of debates on Bill C-207, proposed by the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon), to limit the tenure of senatorial appointments to 10 years. I agree completely with the sentiments that the hon. member wishes to convey to the House concerning the need for general reform in the operations of the other place. In fact, I even agree that some limitation of tenure of our Senators is desirable, if not absolutely necessary, to make the Senate
November 1, 1974

relevant to the political system of this country, in this technologically complex era.
However, I believe that the reforms of the other place required to bring this relevance to Canadian political life are so extensive that the effect of this bill is merely cosmetic and does not provide a fundamental solution to the problem. Therefore I cannot support my hon. colleague on this matter.
I think that perhaps a couple of bills will be required to change the composition of the Senate. Before we talk in terms of 10-year appointments for Senators, we should look at the terms of reference applying to senatorial appointments, and at the function of Senators within the parliamentary process. I therefore propose, in the short time available, to review some of the background of Senate reform and some contemporary responses to the problem.
I remind my hon. colleague that the British North America Act had scarcely passed the experimental stage when, in 1874, the House of Commons was called to consider the desirability of amending the constitution of the Senate. The House was asked to adopt a resolution to the effect that the system of appointment to the Senate was inconsistent with the federal principle, and that the constitution ought to be amended so as to confer upon each province the power of selecting its own senators. Debate on this resolution was adjourned without any action being taken.
Several years later the subject was revived on the motion of the then member for Perth, who advocated abolishing the life tenure of senators, providing a fixed age for compulsory retirement, and limiting "the tenure of one appointment to within the legal term of three parliaments". After debate the motion was withdrawn. In January, 1908, the same member asked for "an age limit for retirement, or a shortened term of service for future senators." Again the debate was adjourned without any action.
In 1909 Sir Richard Scott outlined a broad scheme for reform in the Senate, including the idea that "the term for which senators may be elected or appointed be limited to seven years." Thus the debate over limiting the tenure of senators is not a recent innovation, and is often linked to the question of whether the Senate should be nominated or elected.
At the time of Confederation Canada adopted the Senate nominative system as best suited to the relations which were about to be established between the provinces and the central government. Election was ruled out on the grounds that the government should only be responsible to the House of Commons, the only body to represent the people directly.
The Fathers of Confederation thought the nominative system had definite advantages. Rightly chosen in the true spirit of responsible government, they thought a nominative Senate would be the strongest bulwark of the constitution and the most impartial guardian of true democracy. It would have none of the hereditary weakness of the House of Lords, nor the partisanship of an elected chamber. It could command the services of experts from every walk of life. If it were necessary for its purpose to use the best talents of any profession-to aid in legislation for the
Senate Reform
development of the natural resources of the country, for protecting public health, for extending trade and commerce, or for widening the horizons of citizenship-they were at its disposal.
Since the 1920's no federal government has tried to alter either the powers or the composition of the Senate. However, in the government's proposals to the constitutional conference in February, 1969, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) added Senate reform to his proposals for revision of the federal constitution. The federal proposals envisaged that the Senate be reconstituted to enable it to play a more vital role in reflecting the federal character of the country.
Among other things it was suggested that senators be selected partly by the provinces, with the term of office reduced, perhaps to six years. It was also suggested the Senate be given special powers, including the right to approve federal nominations to the Supreme Court, and to have special legislative responsibility concerning the official languages, human rights, international relations, and other matters. While some of these ideas have been shelved, the question of fixed terms is still very much alive, as we can see by the Prime Minister's remarks during the Throne Speech debate this session.
When the Fathers of Confederation decided to give Senators life tenure, they hoped this would promote the independence of the Senate and, while this may have been the case, it also had the effect of lowering Senators' prestige with the public, who tended to look upon them as a privileged class of old-age pensioners. We all know they are not that. In 1965 the British North America Act was amended, requiring Senators appointed thereafter to retire at 75 years of age. It is interesting to note in passing that this change has lowered the average tenure of a Senator from about 16 years in the early 1960s to an average of eight years by 1971.
Another frequent suggestion is that the appointment of Senators be for a limited term of six, eight or even ten years as in the bill before us. It is argued that more frequent changes of membership might induce greater activity without tending to strengthen the Senate vis-a-vis the House of Commons. Such changes would also increase the introduction of new men and ideas into the Senate but, perhaps what is more important, would mean that any alternation of power between the parties in the Commons could be reflected much sooner in the Senate. That situation would be welcome, instead of the present situation whereby, when a party has been in office for a long time, it will continue to keep its majority in the Senate long after it is defeated in the House.
This is a crucial point. Over the past few years public respect for the legitimate role of the Senate in the parliamentary process has been steadily eroded since we, as members of the Liberal party, have consistently been charged by the Canadian people to govern the nation. This is a responsibility which they have been loathe to give, for good reason I may add, to Her Majesty's loyal opposition.
The present ratio of Liberal Senators to those of other parties is dangerously close to rendering the whole body of the Senate useless. Hence the sincere offer of the Prime Minister to appoint Senators from other parties.

November 1, 1974
Senate Reform
As you can see, Mr. Speaker, it is very difficult to confine oneself to the specific intent of this bill without discussing the whole matter of Senate reform. A simple reduction in the term of senatorial appointments does nothing to answer criticisms of New Democratic Party members, many past members of which party should have continued their very real contribution to the Canadian political system in the Senate after their years in the House of Commons were ended.
I can think of many past NDP members of this House who deserve to be given the nation-wide forum that is accorded to members of the red chamber. Indeed, I can think of a few present members of that party who would be equally effective in the other place.
During debate on the throne speech, I wish to remind the hon. member for Victoria, the Prime Minister suggested the duration of senatorial appointments should be limited to a certain number of years, seven for example, with the option of re-appointing Senators "when they have well served their country".
While most newspapers agreed that the Prime Minister was right to contemplate reform of the Senate, there were many queries concerning this idea. For example, the Toronto Star argued that the greatest value of the Senate lies in the fact that it includes a certain number of strong minded men, not too confined by party ties, who are not afraid to express their views on national affairs and to criticize the government. I quote from the October 18 edition of the Toronto Star:
The danger of the proposed seven-year renewable term is that it would create strong temptation for the Prime Minister of the day to drop these independent, troublesome individuals when their terms expired and to re-appoint only the faithful party hacks who have served the party, if not their country, well. And the remaining members would be under notice not to rock the boat if they wanted their appointments renewed.
The Toronto Star should realize by now that the Liberal party is never quite that partisan and I doubt whether we have ever appointed someone, to use its derogatory phrase, who is a mere "party hack". Rather, we have appointed people who have contributed to the political and social fabric of Canadian society.
At this point I wish to digress and comment on some of the remarks of the hon. member for Victoria. I regret the hon. member feels that, once appointed, Senators should fade away in the lush splendour of the red chamber. I feel that Senators are expected to participate in the political process to the full. I believe that election campaigns are part of the political process.
I can only conclude that the hon. member's derogatory remarks concerning some of our Senators is sour grapes, and perhaps reflects his displeasure that Tory Senators do not participate fully in the Conservative caucus and the Conservative party. However, I do not know that for sure.
Most Senators are partisan appointees and I expect that they continue their partisan involvement. I remind the hon. member that Senators are members of parliament as are members of the House of Commons. We were certainly reminded of that recently in caucus.

Having briefly outlined some theoretical arguments for and against limited tenure for Senators, it is perhaps necessary to consider some practical problems in changing the present situation. The method of appointing Senators is established by the British North America Act, and in over 100 years the only major change in provisions relating to the Senate was the reform of 1965 providing for a compulsory retirement age of 75 years.
Despite this change the fact remains that effective Senate reform is not an easy task, and the Senate cannot be reformed without its consent. Therefore it is important to consider whether the Senate would favour fixed terms of office for its members. The Prime Minister has discussed this with the leader of the government in the Senate, and expressed the hope that some progress can be made in this area.
Yet only two years ago an extensive study of the constitution was undertaken by a joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons. The committee included 11 Senators representing both parties, and it examined at some length the question of appointment and representation in the Senate. Among other things it recommended a new distribution of seats which would maintain 24 seats for Quebec and Ontario, but would allot 12 seats each to British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba; 10 seats each to New Brunswick and Nova Scotia; six seats to Newfoundland, four seats to Prince Edward Island, and two each to the Yukon and Northwest Territories, for a total of 130 seats.
It also recommended that Senators continue to be appointed by the federal government, although one half of the vacancies in each province or territory would be chosen from a panel of nominees submitted by the appropriate provincial or territorial government. It did not, however, recommend a fixed term of appointment for Senators, concluding only that the compulsory retirement age should be lowered to 70 years, and that upon retirement Senators should retain the right to their title and precedence, as well as the opportunity to participate in the work of the Senate or its committees, but not to vote or receive the indemnity of Senators.
Since this recent document, agreed to by a number of Senators, did not propose fixed terms, one is justified in asking if such an idea would find acceptance in the Senate? If not, then all the theoretical arguments for and against the idea become academic, and the question of Senate reform will probably be postponed once again.

subsubtopic: BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT, 1867 AMENDMENT TO LIMIT TENURE OF SENATORS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon) expressed the hope the House would give second reading to this bill this afternoon and send it to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs. He is a nice fellow and I do not like to disappoint him, but I can think of nothing that would be more wasteful of the time of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs than for it to have this bill presented to it.
That is not to say, despite my well-known opposition to the continuance of the Senate, that one can forever block discussion on Senate reform. However, I submit that this particular proposal is not worth committee consideration. I find it just as useless as the proposal of the Prime
November 1, 1974

Minister (Mr. Trudeau) that there be seven year terms, subject to re-appointment.
This bill does not get at the root of the question as to whether the Senate is a desirable and useful part of our parliamentary institution. It is being demonstrated more and more that its practices are not in keeping with the principles of democracy. I contend that unless somebody can come up with more significant and more useful proposals for reform than we have from the hon. member for Victoria and from the Prime Minister, my proposal still stands as number one; let's abolish it.
It always interest me when a member like the hon. member for Victoria talks about the purpose of the Senate. He said its purpose was to give sober second thought to legislation passed by the House of Commons. I always wince a bit when that is said. The implication is that the thought in this House is not sober. I do not accept that at all. In any event, I wonder where the idea came from Mr. Speaker. I do not find it in the British North America Act.
I am sure what I shall read from the British North America Act has been put on the pages of Hansards on previous occasions, but not for a long time. Since there is this talk about the purpose of the Senate, perhaps it might be a good idea to remind ourselves what the Fathers of Confederation had in mind.
Section 23 of the BNA Act reads as follows:
The qualification of a Senator should be as follows:
(1)	He shall be of the full age of thirty years.
I suppose that was reasonable 100 years ago but it certainly discriminates against young people who rightly believe they are quite important in today's generation; they have voting rights at the age of 18 and they have the right to enter this House at the age of 18. At any rate, that is one of the qualifications of a Senator. You must be an old man of thirty.
Note, also, that the Act just says "He". Once upon a time the judicial committee of the Privy Council had to rule that for the purpose of going to the Senate a woman was a person. That was an historic decision of the judicial committee of the Privy Council, and I think it is interesting that related to the history of the Senate was the question whether or not persons to be appointed to that place had to be men only or whether they could include women. I move on. The section continues;
(2)	He shall be either a natural-born subject of the Queen-
I always like that phrase and wonder what would be meant by "un-naturally born".
-or a subject of the Queen naturalized by an act of the Parliament of Great Britain, or of the Parliament of the United Kingdom, Great Britain and Ireland, or of the Legislature of one of the Provinces of Upper Canada, Lower Canada, Canada, Nova Scotia or New Brunswick, before the union, or of the Parliament of Canada, after the union.
Well, those are routine qualifications. Let us go on to subsection (3):
He shall be legally or equitably seised as of freehold for his own use and benefit of lands or tenements held in free and common socage-

I have been asking my learned friends around here what that means, and they are no more learned than I am. Anyway, there it is socage.
-or seised, or possessed for his own use and benefit of lands or tenements held in francalleu or in roture within the province for which he is appointed, of the value of four thousand dollars, over and above all rents, dues, debts, charges, mortgages and incumbrances due or payable out of or charged on or affecting the same.
Boy! If you are going to apply for a job in the other place, you really have to read the fine print.
(4)	His real and personal property shall be together worth four thousand dollars over and above his debts and liabilities.
I am sure that if the hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Gillies) were to move an amendment to the BNA Act he is so concerned about inflation he would hardly consider letting that $4,000 figure still stand as a sufficient requirement to get into the other place.

The hon. member says it is much too low. Does he want to make it $40,000? Or $400,000? In my view any monetary consideration at all is a violation of the basic concept of democracy.
(5)	He shall be resident in the province for which he is appointed;
(6)	In the case of Quebec he shall have his real property qualification in the electoral division for which he is appointed, or shall be resident in that division.
I have been looking through the BNA Act and I find there are no other qualifications required. I do not see any reference to qualifications in terms of intelligence, capacity of training not even sobriety. You just have to be an old man of thirty, a proper subject of the realm and in possession of certain property.

subsubtopic: BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT, 1867 AMENDMENT TO LIMIT TENURE OF SENATORS
speechtext: And be a good party worker.

subsubtopic: BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT, 1867 AMENDMENT TO LIMIT TENURE OF SENATORS
speechtext:
The hon. member for Don Valley says "and be a good party worker". That is not in the Act, but that has certainly been the case in the last 100 years or more. The bill before us makes a proposal under which a term in the Senate could come to an end. I would remind the sponsor that there are already provisions in the BNA Act for the place of a Senator to become vacant. These are to be found in section 31:
The place of a Senator shall become vacant in any of the following cases:
(1)	If for two consecutive sessions of the parliament he fails to give his attendance in the Senate.
Well, Their Honours do manage to get into the place, so that rule really does not apply very often.
(2)	If he takes an oath or makes a declaration or acknowledgment of allegiance, obedience or adherence to a foreign power, or does an act whereby he becomes a subject or citizen, or entitled to the rights or privileges of a subject or citizen, of a foreign power;
(3)	If he is adjudged bankrupt or insolvent or applies for the benefit of any law relating to insolvent debtors, or becomes a public defaulter;
I do not know what the definition of that last word might be. Anyway, there it is, in the Act, and it is printed with a capital "D".
(4)	If he is attainted of treason or convicted of felony or of any infamous crime.

Who is to define what is infamous? I believe there are persons guilty of things I would regard as infamous but which might seem a cause for reward to others.
(5)	If he ceases to be qualified in respect of property or of residence; provided that a Senator shall not be deemed to have ceased to be qualified in respect of residence by reason only of his residing at the seat of the Government of Canada while holding an office under that government requiring his presence there.
There is really nothing else in the BNA Act regarding the qualifications of a Senator. It does not say he must have gone to school, or hold a university degree, or hold a certificate of professional proficiency. He simply has to be a person past thirty, a proper citizen, not a public defaulter, and possess a certain amount of property.
Some limitations are imposed on Senators. The main limitation is that they cannot introduce into the Senate a bill involving the expenditure of money or the imposition of a tax. There is the further provision that though Their Honours can amend almost any bill we send over there, they cannot amend a supply bill; they must either accept it or reject it in total.
I find these things about the other place interesting, but one searches in vain for the qualification to which reference is made most often, namely, that Senators are appointed to give a sober second thought to what goes on in the House of Commons. I would therefore suggest to the hon. member for Victoria that, before he presses too far his conviction that the Senate is not doing what it was designed to do, he should produce a blueprint setting out what he thinks it was designed for, and in the absence of such a blueprint it seems to me the other place has developed along lines which are natural for a body made up of persons appointed by the government of the day.
It just so happens that during most of this century the Liberals have been in power and they have been filling tl\e place with their appointees. But had the reverse been the case, and had the Tories been in power I doubt there would have been much difference in the performance of Tory Senators.

speechtext: They would be more sober.

subsubtopic: BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT, 1867 AMENDMENT TO LIMIT TENURE OF SENATORS
speechtext:
The hon. member says they would be more sober. That is his comment, not mine. In any case, as I have said on many occasions, I do have respect for many of the Senators over there. I know a number of them personally. After all, I have been around here longer than most of them. I know them and I respect the 25 or 30 of them who have worked hard at the job. But it seems to me that the whole set-up, couched as it is in the language of 1867, does not fit in with a modern democracy where parliament is supposed to be the body responsible to the people of this country.
I have said many a time that we in the House of Commons can and do make mistakes. But when we make mistakes we have to go back and answer for those mistakes, even as we answer for the things we do correctly, to the people who sent us here in the first place. Over in the Senate, whether they do the right thing, the wrong thing, or nothing at all, they are not responsible to anyone. They

are not even responsible to the Prime Minister who recommended their appointment in the first place.
Therefore, Madam Speaker, I submit that the sensible thing for a modern twentieth century parliament to do is to decide that we believe in democracy, and that we want the persons who make the laws of this country to be elected by, and made responsible to, the people of Canada.
Usually if I find myself in a discussion with students and others, and that particular word comes up and it is said that the lawmakers should be elected, someone will ask: "Well, what about electing the Senate?" I say, let the matter rest rather than that. We have enough conflicts now between the parties in this House, between the executive and the members of this House, between Ottawa and the provinces, that if we added to that the conflict between two houses each with the authority to stand on its own feet, it would slow down the process of government even more. So if we cannot get rid of the Senate, let us leave it as it is.
The Senate is in a situation in which Their Honours realize that their authority is limited. As the hon. member for Victoria has pointed out, in the last parliament the Senate did object to a clause in one of the bills we sent over to them. He indicated why he thought they did that, but at any rate they did realize that once this House of Commons had confirmed its previous vote there was nothing more for them to do.
As I say, if we cannot get rid of the place altogether I think it should be kept in the situation it is in at the present time, where the Senators say their piece once in a while but really do not try to upset the democratic apple cart.
I should like to make a brief reference again to the fact that some of the committees in the other place do a good job. The reports they have produced have been the result of thorough and exhaustive study, and some of their recommendations have been exceedingly worth while. But I do not think that the fact that 25 or 30 persons do a good job when work is assigned to them is justification for keeping 102 persons on the payroll; and not only on the payroll, but nominally with the authority to veto the decisions made by the elected representatives.
So, Madam Speaker, I am afraid, like a good Conservative of long ago, I am unrevised and unrepentant about this issue. I think that in the democracy of this latter part of the twentieth century we should be democrats all the way, and that we should have a parliament that is made up only of those who are responsible to the people. Therefore that means getting rid of the Senate. I suggest that to waste time on this kind of reform is just that-a waste of time.

Madam Speaker, may I begin by congratulating you upon your attainment of office and on the way you conduct that important office. I wish you well in your duties.
I listened with great delight to that champion of the status quo, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). He reads the British North America Act to us just as they say Senator Huey Long used to read the cookbooks to the U.S. Senate when he was conducting a filibuster. I will not show any preference between the

books, but I must say I prefer the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre to Senator Long.
I do not want the hon. member of the Liberal party, whose seat I do not know since I do not have my seating plan with me, to think that I am registering an attitude of sour grapes; that is not so at all. Also, my own colleagues will know that I am not revealing any conflict of interest or anticipating things that never seem to come. But I will say to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre that I will support his stand on the Senate when I reach the age of 74 VL At that time I will give in and support him; but since I am only 55, the same age as the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), we will have to let hope spring a bit reluctantly from time to time, if not eternally.
I believe this proposal is perhaps the oldest public discussion. In 1893, long before I was born, before the mover of this motion was born, and even before the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre was born, there was a big political convention in Ottawa, the first national convention in the nation's history. The Liberal party met, and one of the resolutions was that we should reform the Senate. As I say, that was in 1893 and there has not been much reforming done since then.
The giant step taken a few years ago was to say that the Senators could go until they were 75 and no longer, and that has changed the place a good deal. We read of the distinguished Senator who made two speeches in all his career. When he first went there he denied he did so as a matter of political patronage. The next speech was when he thanked his colleagues for giving him a painting on his one hundredth birthday-and there were 35 years between the two speeches. Nevertheless, they said he was a most excellent man, and while he did not speak he always voted for the party whenever those Senate bells began their gentle ringing.
And so the Senate is sometimes laughed at, Mr. Speaker. Dawson, at page 314, talks about the impossibility of making much change, and he quotes from Ulysses:
Surely, slumber is more sweet than toil, the shore Than labour in the deep mid-ocean, wind, and wave, and oar; Oh rest ye, brother mariners, we will not wander more.
And they practise that urge toward tranquility which keeps the body alive and functioning.
On the other hand I think the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is a bit cynical in suggesting, as he often does, that the contribution of some of the Senators is not sufficient to justify the continued existence of the institution. In my short 17 years here-and I came long after the hon. member-I have been much impressed by the work of the committee on the Caribbean-Common-wealth-Canada commission, one of the finest studies ever done in that very important area, as well as by the poverty study. Some other excellent work has been done in the realm of external affairs which was very, very useful. In fact, I should like to see the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre go to that place; he would add a lot to it.

I have often thought that if I cannot get into the Senate then perhaps a university degree, a doctor of letters or something, will do. I will accept his offer and not consign the hon. member to the Senate. Perhaps it will be the leader of his party who will go there, because the leader of the NDP fought very hard against my party during the campaign. I heard him attacking the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield), and I think he was motivated by fear. He thought that we were going to get a majority government, and the NDP had been in bed with the Liberals for so long that they could not bear the thought of sleeping alone. Thus they did not want a majority government, so that should come as some reward.
To turn to the bill of the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon), I do congratulate him on what I think is a very sensible suggestion for reform. I agree profoundly with him that neither that House nor this can sustain a continued lack of respect among the public. I have always said that as individuals we can live with that old syndrome of politicians with all their peculiarities, but there must be a basic respect for the institution itself.
The manner in which the hon. member has put forward this step in reform, and as a member of a reform minded party I am all for it and do not join with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre in his unrelenting support of the status quo, I think is forward and progressive. I support the hon. member for Victoria most fully and heartily. In my mind he has made a good move and I wish him well.
A very difficult step in legislation is that of getting the second House different enough to be worth while. As I said long ago, if it disagrees with this House it is inequi-tous, and if it agrees it is superfluous. So you have to find some way, and I think the hon. member has opened a good line in that direction. I would suggest perhaps that if we had 10 members from each province it would be a better place, particularly for example from Prince Edward Island.
Before I take my seat, as I know other hon. members want to speak, I want to point out that the Prime Minister, I am sure accidentally, misled the country and the province of Prince Edward Island when he said through the throne speech that he had talked to Senator Flynn, and that in any case where a member of the Conservative party retired he would appoint a Conservative in his place. I happen to recall that Senator J. J. MacDonald of Prince Edward Island, a Progressive Conservative, retired in 1971

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I regret very much that there are only a few minutes left as I know there are a number of members who would like to make a contribution, some of them members on this side of the House.
I listened to the crusade for reform by the hon. member who just spoke and I could not help but remember that the hon. member for Laprairie (Mr. Watson) and I represent constituencies both of which have far more people resident in them than are resident in the entire province of the hon. member which is now represented in this place by four parliamentarians and in the other place also by four. I cannot believe he was serious in suggesting that we should increase such numbers to 10. If he wants to start on reform I think he should start in his own house and look at it a little more closely.
The hon. member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon) presented himself as having two bills, and I think the one to deal with the question of representation genuinely involves the problem of reform. I agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) that this bill is not reform and does not get to the heart of the matter.
The real problem with the other place is the lack of opposition. The opposition has dwindled to a handful, and many of them are aging and are not as forceful as they were in other years.
I listened to the hon. member who proposed this bill complain about political partisanship. I wish he had been a candidate in the election of 1962, as I was, when the Senators in the other place had a slightly different preponderance of numbers. I can remember Senator Grosart doing something somewhat similar to the job that Senator Keith Davey performed in the last election. All that time there were members on this side of the House who had some misgivings about the degree of partisanship involved.
If political partisanship is a crime then there is something wrong with our political life. Surely the very essence of our political life is a healthy interest in the democratic process. The cure lies in a better and stronger opposition in the Senate, where there should be a better balance of the parties in Canada. The real weakness of the Senate is the lack of a parliamentary opposition. That is the point to which the hon. member who moved this bill should have directed his remarks.
I listened to the arguments of the hon. member for Victoria, and at no point did he deal with the basic point of his bill; that is, limiting the length of a Senate term. This is a popular exercise and I submit that limiting the term would bring about, if it were enacted-and I do not

believe it will be enacted in this form-a discrimination against younger men in the other place. The problem of accepting a limited appointment, to those who are in a profession or business career and are younger in years, is a very serious one indeed.
We are, in my opinion, very correctly raising the question of conflict of interest. We are saying to the men and women who go to the other place they must serve full time, they must serve without conflict of interest, and they must cut their former ties. A man or woman who leaves a profession, business or usual activity, for a limited period, at the end of that period has to face the certainty of going back into civilian life, as it were, and at that point in too many cases has to start thinking of bread and butter.
In such circumstances the very quality of independence, the very quality of full-time service, and the very quality of making sure there is no conflict of interest comes, shall I say, under pressure. That is not the point. The point is that we have a Senate at this stage, whatever the faults of the system may be, and I will concede there are a number of faults. The fact is that the independence of the Senate is the very guarantee of its integrity. The amendment which is proposed in this bill does not, in my opinion, deal with it.
There are two committees about to be struck in this House; one is a joint committee of the other place and the House of Commons to deal with the Public Service of Canada, and the other will deal with the National Capital Region. We look to the other place for able and continuing representation by parliamentarians who will persist in taking an interest in these matters.
On October 30, 1972, there was a previous parliament, of which I was a member, with a number of faces that are not now here, some 120 of them. The turnover of elected representatives in the Canadian parliament is very great indeed. The other place has provided continuity on a number of committees dealing with a number of important matters.
I should like at this stage, with the indulgence of the House and if I have time, to tell a short anecdote. I regret that the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefen-baker) is not here. I am thinking of the problem of the lost statues.
When I was a member of a previous parliament the then minister of public works, now a member of the other place, called upon one or two of the local members, Jean Richard and myself, and said: "I have a problem and I would like local members to give me their very best advice. What do you do with certain statues?" One of them was a statue of former Prime Minister Meighen, and it was simply outrageous. It was not done by any Liberal artist; it was no Grit plot and there was no attempt at concealment, but what you would do with such a statue is utterly beyond my comprehension.
